#1564. 'I have something unresolved': Ole Gunnar Solskjaer piles more pressure on old pal Michael Carrick as he says he WOULD manage Man United again - despite trying to back him to succeed

By LUKE AUGUSTUS, ASSISTANT SPORTS EDITOR

Published: 03:52 EDT, 2 November 2026 | Updated: 05:42 EDT, 2 November 2026

Ole Gunnar Solskjaer has admitted that he would be interested in returning as Manchester United manager in the future as he has 'something unresolved'.

Pressure is mounting on current head coach Michael Carrick as the Red Devils' dismal season continues to go from bad to worse.

After losing 2-0 at Chelsea on Saturday afternoon, United sit 17th in the Premier League - only above 18th-placed Crystal Palace on goal difference and just two points ahead of bottom side Sunderland.

Solskjaer has been in the Old Trafford hotseat before with his own path mirroring Carrick's from being an interim manager initially to becoming a permanent appointment.

The Norwegian had Carrick among his backroom staff before he was sacked as United boss in November 2021. When Ruben Amorim was sacked in January, both were interviewed as interim successors before Carrick was chosen.

And speaking about taking the reins at United in the future, Solskjaer revealed he would accept it.

Ole Gunnar Solskjaer (left) has revealed he would like to manage Manchester United in the future but backs current head coach Michael Carrick (right) to overturn the club's fortunes

Pressure is growing on Carrick which increased following Saturday's 2-0 defeat at Chelsea

Solskjaer was sacked as United manager in November 2021 after nearly three years in charge

'Going back to what has been is not always as good,' he told Norwegian outfit TV2.

'Yes, I had lined up [as Manchester United's interim manager last season], but I didn't think it would last longer than the summer. It was probably time for someone else to try.

'I also feel like I have something unresolved. Of course it would have been nice to have the opportunity again.'

Elaborating further, Solskjaer was keen to stress that he is not looking to oust his former United team-mate and friend Carrick.

'If Michael does well for 10 years and decides to quit, and they ask me if I can take them for two months, of course I wouldn't say no. I've been at that club for 18-19 years, so it's part of the family. But it's not something I'm thinking about.'

Despite growing scrutiny on Carrick, Solskjaer is adamant that the under-fire head coach can turn around the club's fortunes.

'Michael has what it takes to take that club forward. I think he's the right man. He understands the club, understands the fans and knows what's needed.'

Proof will be in the pudding with Carrick preparing his side for Tuesday's Champions League clash with Roma and then Sunday's Premier League encounter versus Aston Villa, both at Old Trafford, before the international break.

#1561. De Roon: “I never had any doubts about joining Roma.”

Marten De Roon gave an interview to Idealista.it in which he discussed his arrival in Rome.

“When the coach called me, I already knew it would be a difficult move, partly because of the history of Roma and Atalanta, partly because of my history with Roma on social media; but at a certain point we had made up our minds, I had no doubts. The pitch speaks for itself. I had no doubts; I wanted to prove on the pitch my desire to be here. Gasperini is also demonstrating this; facts count, there’s time.”

The Dutch midfielder explained how he experiences football: “In two different ways. On the pitch, I want to win at all costs. My main quality, what I like to do, is to see the game. I’m tactically prepared, it’s my strength: I see where we can attack well, where we can defend better. From midfield, I like to manage the team, call the markers. Off the pitch, I like to joke, talk, and, above all, observe. I like trying to help my teammates; I’m a professional, and even off the pitch, I try to be helpful, given my age and experience.”

The former Atalanta player spoke about the Giallorossi dressing room: “There are a lot of nice people. I’m still finding my role, so I don’t joke around too much, but the atmosphere is healthy; it seems like an ‘easy’ dressing room. Years ago, I thought it was a very difficult dressing room, even playing against them; now I’ve come in and I’ve seen that it’s healthy, warm, and welcoming. I already knew some of them, obviously Malen, Rensch, Mancini, Gollini, and Cristante. This obviously helps; it’s made things easier.”

De Roon gave a behind-the-scenes look at how he looked for a place to live in the capital: “I spoke to the guys here in the locker room, Pellegrini helped me get to know the city, he gave me a hand with so many things, together with the club.”

Marten De Roon spoke about his relationship with Gasperini: “We spent eight years together, we had the best time with Atalanta, we fought so many battles together, and I’ve always thanked him. Our relationship is above all professional; if he’s your coach, you don’t see him off the pitch during the week. Last year, he called me every now and then, asking about Malen, but more than anything he wanted confirmation; he was already convinced. I had no doubts. He’s doing pretty well, right?”

At Trigoria, medical staff are resorting to infiltrations in an attempt to allow the goalkeeper to recover in time for the match at the Olimpico.

His condition will be monitored until the final hours, but Devis Vásquez remains ready to start. This would mark the Colombian’s return to Serie A since his last appearance, on May 25, 2025, when he wore the Empoli jersey.

There are no particular concerns regarding Gianluca Mancini, who did not participate in the resumption training session due to a simple workload management issue.

The defender remains available and will compete for a starting spot alongside Balerdi ahead of the match against Sassuolo. Gasperini will therefore have to resolve several doubts before finalizing the starting eleven, especially in midfield and goal.

#1557. Liverpool's anonymous attackers cost them the chance of beating Arsenal despite dominant display... the gap to the champions is narrowing - but the Reds still aren't close enough, writes LEWIS STEELE

Published: 21:00 EDT, 1 November 2026 | Updated: 06:06 EDT, 2 November 2026

As disheartened fans spilled out of Anfield, nearly all conversations were about the referee and questions over why he did not point to the penalty spot in the first half when Jurrien Timber pulled back Alexander Isak.

They had a point and this game would have been completely different had Andy Madley – or VAR Stuart Attwell – seen what everyone else saw when Isak was an inch short of connecting with a header and possible goal because he was pulled back by his marker.

It was a similar situation to Liverpool’s only other defeat under new boss Andoni Iraola, where supporters were left aggrieved at the incorrect call to send off Ryan Gravenberch against Manchester City.

In both cases they were unlucky to be on the wrong side of refereeing mistakes and would have cursed the fine margins. But in both cases Reds fans will also realise their team just did not do enough to win too.

Just like against City, Liverpool dominated Arsenal for large parts of this match. It felt as though they were one magic moment or opposition mistake away from scoring and lfiting off the Anfield roof.

But in both cases, that moment never materialised. It felt like the Liverpool attackers were looking around waiting for somebody else to step up and be the man to start the pendulum swinging in Liverpool’s favour.

Alexander Isak and Liverpool's attackers struggled against Arsenal's defence

They had zero shots on target, according to Opta, and that is the only statistic that Iraola will be mulling over in the coming days.

Bradley Barcola, Florian Wirtz and Alexander Isak have all been frighteningly good in recent weeks but in this game, especially the second half, Liverpool’s big-money forwards looked like they had run out of ideas.

Arsenal defended like their lives depended on it and their away fans, who barely saw the ball down their end of the pitch after half-time, celebrated every Gabriel header or David Raya catch like a goal.

The home team, meanwhile, were left throwing long balls forward to Virgil van Dijk – the only player who could aerially compete with Arsenal’s team of giants. It felt like several Hail Mary passes but no one could answer Iraola’s prayers.

Liverpool’s two defeats to City and now Arsenal both demonstrate the gap between Iraola’s outfit and a genuine title contender. There is definitely a small level between Liverpool and Arsenal – but Reds fans can take solace in knowing it is not a chasm like last season.

A referee decision here, a better final ball there and Liverpool may be still unbeaten under Iraola and the whole country would consider them a title contender.

Iraola has closed the gap on the top teams but knows several tweaks are still needed to take that next step. Can they do it this season? It is far from impossible but seems a tall order.

The upcoming fixture list is kinder to them, at least. Of the current top eight, Liverpool have played all of them – two in the Carabao Cup – and won each test apart from City and Arsenal. The next two league games are against teams in 18th and 17th.

Florian Wirtz has improved recently but was unable to provide cutting edge on Sunday

But right now, Liverpool are a team with too many ‘ifs’, ‘buts’ and ‘maybes’. If Alexis Mac Allister did not get under a first-half header that looked like a certain goal… if the referee had given a clear foul on Isak… if the forwards packed their shooting boots.

As it was, for all of the nail-biting moments for Mikel Arteta on the touchline as Liverpool had lots of the ball in the final third, his goalkeeper David Raya could have had a cigar in and read the papers for most of the second half.

That is what will bother Iraola the most.

As for being a complete team able to compete for the league title again, Liverpool seem so close yet so far.

Trey Nyoni made his first Premier League start and it will not be his last after he put in a solid shift.

Though he misplaced some passes and was probably lucky to escape an early yellow card after two late challenges, the 19-year-old presents Iraola with an interesting tactical quirk.

The Englishman always wants the ball and drops into the back line to start attacks, with a maturity beyond his years.

He sits deep which allows Alexis Mac Allister to play as more of a box-to-box midfielder, undoubtedly his best position.

So where does this leave Ryan Gravenberch, who spent the afternoon on the bench? Given the amount of games Liverpool have across competitions, the Dutchman will still play many minutes — but he is currently at risk of falling down the pecking order thanks to the exciting talent of Nyoni.

There is also a conversation to be had about how Liverpool’s balance and control was lost when Nyoni was replaced by Dominik Szoboszlai.

Trey Nyoni excelled for the Reds and helped the home side control the tempo

Casual football fans who maybe only tune in for the big games have never seen Wirtz play well.

They must wonder what all the fuss is about.

The German has been on fine form in recent weeks but has been like a ghost — no Halloween pun intended — in the two biggest matches against City and Arsenal.

It is all well and good performing against teams like LASK in the Champions League but Wirtz, at £116million, was signed to make a difference in these blockbuster clashes.

Instead, his national team colleague Kai Havertz continued his record of impacting the games that really matter come May. How Wirtz could do with some of that killer instinct.

#1552. Crystanbul revisited: The night Liverpool’s title hopes spectacularly fell apart

When you think back to Liverpool’s stunning collapse to surrender the 2013-14 Premier League title, chances are you remember the Steven Gerrard slip.

That came with three games to go. Chelsea were the visitors and Gerrard’s untimely loss of footing allowed Demba Ba to run through and score.

The west London side would go on to win the game 2-0, with Jose Mourinho banging the Chelsea badge on his blue gilet in front of the away fans.

To mark the Year of the Horse, we tell Chelsea-related tales from previous such cycles in the Lunar New Year… 👀🐎 https://t.co/cxtAKVaSqV

— Chelsea FC (@ChelseaFC) February 17, 2026

But if the loss to Chelsea was the dagger in the heart of Liverpool’s title bid, the next game was the decapitation.

At a time when cooler heads were struggling to prevail, it was hard to see Liverpool’s loss to Chelsea as anything but gift-wrapping the Premier League trophy to Manchester City.

In reality, Liverpool still had a decent chance of winning their first league title in 24 years.

After the Chelsea game, Liverpool had dropped from top spot but only on goal difference with City now leading. The two teams had kept a similar scoring pacing, both nearing 100, but City’s defence had been stronger, giving them a 12-goal difference over their Merseyside opponents.

The path to victory for Liverpool then was to win both games and hope City dropped points or to win by such a margin that they swing the goal difference in their favour.

It wasn’t an unrealistic prospect either, City did have the harder fixtures. While they had two home games, they faced two teams in Aston Villa and West Ham that were yet to be mathematically clear of relegation.

Liverpool meanwhile knew that if they got through the game against Palace, they would play the final match of the season at Anfield against a Newcastle side that was safe in ninth but had a minus 18 goal difference, the worst in the top half of the table.

If given the choice, Brendan Rodgers may well have chosen Palace as the team he fancied to face at this point of the season. They were 11th and already confirmed their place in the Premier League next season. Selhurst Park is about 40 miles away from the coast but Palace should already be on the beach.

Palace were on a good run of form, winning their previous five out of six, but surely, surely Liverpool would comfortably knock them over.

If there was ever a man born to ruin a party, it was Pulis. After the Chelsea defeat, Rodgers complained about the defensive tactics deployed by Mourinho. Pulis probably sat in his wingback armchair at home and a smile appeared across his lips.

The fixture had been selected for the Monday night, meaning Steven Gerrard led his Liverpool team out into the setting South London sun with a point to prove.

The initial focus was on Gerrard. How would the man who was as Liverpool as the Beatles and turning K into Ch when speaking recover from being the man who may have cost them the Premier League title?

That answer was given very quickly. In front of a Crystal Palace stand full of fans that were very clearly up for it, Gerrard whipped in a corner to an unmarked Joe Allen at the back post. The smallest man on the pitch scored against a defence that had not conceded a set-piece goal all season.

The first half ran out as exactly as Liverpool would have hoped. They had 68% of the ball, 12 shots to Palace’s three and were in complete control, much to Pulis’ annoyance.

He told the BBC later that year that he gave his centre-halves Scott Dann and Damien Delaney a b*llocking for not getting close enough to Luis Suarez and Daniel Sturridge, which is easier said than done.

The words of wisdom appeared to go in one ear and out the other as Liverpool scored two quick goals to begin the second half.

Sterling skipped away from the pressure of Joel Ward while both Dann and Delaney had dropped deep to cover the run of Suarez.

The two got closer to tackling each other as Sturridge’s effort deflected off Delaney’s trailing foot and past a helpless Julian Speroni.

Remembering his manager’s half-time words, Delaney soon charges out to try and close down Suarez just past the centre circle in Palace’s half.

His horror show of a second half continues as he instead controls it for Suarez before being completely wrong-footed as the Uruguayan charges at the two Palace defenders now left.

Raheem Sterling was on hand to relieve the pass and pull Dann away from Suarez and even with the English winger’s pass being completely underhit, Dann misses it and Suarez gets it through Speroni’s legs on the way to the net.

Liverpool smelt blood, but in many ways the quick nature of their two goals proved to be their demise.

Rodgers revealed the message at half-time was just to win and that “if it’s 1-0, it’s 1-0.” but asking for calm heads at this time was too much for a team that had been feeding off euphoria.

Ahead of the Chelsea game, Liverpool had won their last 10 Premier League games. They had led the league for the past four weeks and 24 years of pent-up frustration had morphed into a feeling of this finally being the year, of it being destiny. For a long while, Rodgers and the players harnessed that feeling.

This was not just any team either, for you would be hard-pressed to find another city in England where football is more woven into the fabric than it is in Liverpool. They had suffered at the hands of Manchester United and now they needed it to be their turn.

That pandemonium was going through the players’ minds when Suarez raced to grab the ball at 3-0.

It was a powder keg ready to explode and the Selhurst Park faithful needed little reason to believe. The spark that set the whole thing ablaze came from the man who had helped gift Liverpool two goals, Damien Delaney.

In pushing forward for more goals, Liverpool had left themselves open at the back. The midfield pair of Gerrard and Lucas were particularly at fault for allowing Delaney to reach just outside the box completely unmarked.

The back four had all dropped deep, prompting Glen Johnson to neither go with his fellow defenders or close down Delaney. Instead, he stood stiff, waited for Delaney to shoot and turned his body sideways in order to protect himself.

Having been the victim of a deflection earlier in the half, Delaney was now the beneficiary of one. The ball came off the stomach of Johnson and went straight into the top left corner.

At the time, Martin Tyler, who was on commentary for Sky, said it would “get the goal difference back for Liverpool” with the possibility of something even worse not yet entering his mind.

Right then, Rodgers should have reacted. He had two experienced centre-backs in Daniel Agger and Kolo Toure sitting on the bench but they remained uncalled for as Liverpool pushed forward once again.

Just a minute later, Liverpool had seven men in the opposition box when Palace’s Yannick Bolasie skipped past the half-hearted tackle from Philippe Coutinho. Johnson again adopted the ‘stand still and hope I get him’ approach, which Bolasie said ‘thank you very much to’ as he knocked it by him.

The Liverpool players did get back but to nowhere useful. Dwight Gayle gave Jon Flanagan a shoulder feint, meaning he had plenty of room to poke home Bolasie’s pass.

You could barely hear the stadium announcer announcing the goal over the sound of the crowd. Palace was up for it. Selhurst Park was up for it. Liverpool were collapsing under the fear of their own nightmare.

This time Rodgers did react, but he only took off Sturridge for Victor Moses who at this point in his career was still a winger.

The midfield two of Lucas and Gerrard were completely bypassed once again as a chipped ball was controlled by the chest of Glenn Murray.

Martin Skrtel had come out to try and get close to Murray, leaving a gaping hole for Gayle. He waited for the ball to bounce before slotting it past Mignolet. The Liverpool collapse was complete.

“Liverpool have caved in,” shouted Tyler. Rodgers had a blank expression on his face, masking what must have been absolute despair on the inside.

The final whistle blew soon after. Liverpool, whose modern history had been built on the overturning of a 3-0 deficit, had just been on the wrong side of that very moment.

Gerrard was on his haunches. Suarez cried into his shirt as he bent over. With that, Liverpool’s title hopes were over.

“There is no doubt Manchester City will go on and win it,” said Rodgers. “We needed to win to keep the pressure on going into the last game and we did not do that.”

Winning the Premier League title would have been the apex of Rodgers’ career. He would have had a figure as beloved as Klopp. Maybe they could have kept hold of Suarez for another year and made a push in the Champions League.

That night in South London completely changed the trajectory of Liverpool Football Club. The always next year team would have to wait another year at least. In the end, they had to wait another six.

Since that night, Liverpool have won 10 times at Selhurst Park, including a 7-0 thumping, and yet Selhurst Park will always be a painful memory.

Nine minutes of madness had defined a whole season in one of the greatest Premier League moments of all time.

#1551. Tottenham look set to deliver after so many disappointments but Roberto De Zerbi's side need a nasty streak if they are to build on their momentum ahead of a daunting festive period, writes RIATH AL-SAMARRAI

By RIATH AL-SAMARRAI, CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER

Published: 06:52 EDT, 1 November 2026 | Updated: 06:31 EDT, 2 November 2026

It was late on Saturday evening when Roberto De Zerbi relayed a few of the comments he had shared with Tottenham’s players at half-time in their 2-0 win over Crystal Palace. One of those remarks was indicative of how quickly things can change.

In the knowledge that his side were 45 minutes away from a rare spot in the upper portion of the table, he reminded them: ‘We can't forget where we have been two weeks ago. Two weeks ago, before the Coventry game, we were last in the table and we can't forget.’

With Tottenham, it is always prudent to know calamity is never too far away, but for the first time in two years, there is a gathering excitement at the club - in the crowd and the dressing room.

The win over Palace was assisted hugely by Jean-Philippe Mateta’s red card after 13 minutes, but Spurs have an uncanny knack of slipping on the easier opportunities. Not this time – goals from Archie Gray and Jan Paul van Hecke punctuated a dominant performance and a third straight win. Three managers and 616 days had expired since the last such streak.

But Spurs appear to be on the march and a promising season is belatedly taking shape. To finally deliver after so many disappointments, there are certain areas where improvements must follow…

Roberto De Zerbi reminded his players of where they had come from during their 2-0 win over Crystal Palace

That was De Zerbi’s own assessment of his frontline after a familiar shortcoming against Palace may have been concealed by the win. It was not lost on him that both of Tottenham’s goals were scored by defenders, nor that they had 34 shots to Palace’s two. As ever, Spurs had abundant creativity in their side but lacked a clinical edge.

De Zerbi said: ‘If we want to follow perfection, we have to be more nasty, no? That is an individual thing, because if I'm number nine, number 10, I want to score. But I can't say nothing.’

He later clarified that comment to encompass the whole side, but it was clear that the onus falls most on Dominic Solanke and Omar Marmoush.

In fairness to the pair, Palace defended so deep after Mateta’s dismissal that they had no space to operate, but one goal apiece this season is a poor return. Solanke, in particular, needs to do a better job of reading the movements and intentions of those around him – too often on Saturday he appeared a thought or two behind Mathys Tel and Mohammed Kudus, who both impressed in the more generous spaces out wide.

De Zerbi wants his side to develop a 'nasty' streak - particularly his attackers

Marmoush is an interesting case for De Zerbi. His mobility and technical ability are clear but he is yet to reveal his best position. On Saturday he was used as a No 10, having already been switched between roles on the left and up front. This experiment drew muted results.

It might be the case that a sustained run in one spot would be beneficial, but for now there appears to be confusion over where to use him. There is also a nagging thought that his best striking potential comes in a two-striker system, as shown in his most prolific period at Frankfurt, but that is not the way De Zerbi plays.

A significant improvement for Tottenham has come in midfield and, specifically, the pairing between Matheus Fernandes and Sandro Tonali.

Acquired at great cost, there was limited patience around the delivery of their impact, but time was always necessary, because De Zerbi’s system is notoriously complicated. In recent weeks, Fernandes and Tonali have shown signs that the penny has dropped on what they have to do.

This has been especially relevant in the instance of Tonali, who is very much the tempo-setter of the side on the ball and off it. On Saturday, he was excellent, or worth ‘double’ in the words of De Zerbi. There were times earlier in the season when he appeared disinterested, as if Tottenham was not the destination he had in mind, but his work rate was brilliant against Palace – he covered 12.3km, won all three of his tackles, and completed 93 per cent of his passes. He was all-action.

The same would be said for Fernandes, who covered 11.6km of ground and finessed a superb cross for Van Hecke’s goal. As a pair with Tonali, he was key to the pressing operation that limited Palace to a single counter-attack in the second half.

Mateus Fernandes (pictured) and Sandro Tonali have been huge boosts in the midfield

De Zerbi struck an interesting note after the game by alluding to the cohesiveness of his side and how it has changed on the pitch. Perhaps that relates to the recent team-bonding exercise in Marbella, but more likely they just needed time to understand the complexities of their manager’s demands.

‘I think even before the international break we were playing well,’ De Zerbi said. ‘We were playing maybe not 90 minutes, but many parts of the game we played very well. We didn't score. We conceded a stupid goal and then we lost energy. We lost spirit. We lost the right union between the players.

‘If we compare Tottenham before the international break and Tottenham after the international break, now we are playing as a team. Before the international break we were playing as many very good players, but not as a team.’

Archie Gray, for one, is getting to grips with the less familiar brief at right-back. The requirements to swap spots with Fernandes, overlap Kudus or hold the advanced position are mind-scrambling, but he has adapted well. His withdrawal at half-time against Palace was down to his first-half yellow card and doesn’t detract from a salient point – he can evidently be trusted to replace Pedro Porro, or at least give the latter scope for a breather.

Tottenham have an opportunity now. Their next four fixtures are Leeds, Ipswich, Sunderland and Fulham, with a nasty run waiting in December and early January.

If they can get something from Elland Road, the other three assignments present a rich opportunity for momentum before the tricky festive period.

One key area to improve in the short term will come against defensive sides who offer less space. That Spurs scored only twice from 80 per cent possession against Palace highlighted the issue.

De Zerbi said: ‘We are improving in the principle and the quality of play. Maybe we are not ready yet to play against such a low block but maybe in two or three months we will be.’

#1549. First Anfield victory for 14 years was vindication for Mikel Arteta after Fleetwood humbling. His Arsenal look the finished article - Liverpool were authors of their own downfall, writes OLIVER HOLT

Published: 13:54 EDT, 1 November 2026 | Updated: 06:32 EDT, 2 November 2026

Five nights ago, 40 miles to the north of Anfield at a remote outpost of English football, Arsenal fell to one of the most humiliating reverses of their long and august history. In the teeth of a gale that blew in off the Irish Sea, they were knocked out of the League Cup by Fleetwood Town, a team 18th in League Two.

They left with their tails between their legs, their teenage prodigy Max Dowman sent off in a melee, their heart questioned, their quality debated, their discipline an issue. Mikel Arteta and his side knew that just a few days later, at the other end of the Fylde Coast and across the Ribble Estuary, they would have to swap running the gauntlet of the Cod Army for the challenge of facing down the roar of the Kop.

They did not shirk it. If Tuesday night was a humbling, their gritty 1-0 victory in an Anfield that was a cauldron once more felt like a significant triumph. It was a defensive masterclass from the champions, an exercise in indomitability. It was their first victory here since 2012 and it took them above Manchester City so that they sit, once more, at the top of the table. Liverpool could not summon a single shot on target.

‘It felt like the end of the world when we were knocked out at Fleetwood,’ Arteta said after this win. ‘You look so silly. I was thinking “How can I lift these players up?” You have to dig deep. This was a mission to win here and it is something that we have not done for 14 years for a variety of reasons. We knew we would have to navigate some difficult moments.’

If Arteta left Fleetwood answering questions about his management of Dowman, he finished this game by striding on to the pitch after the final whistle, pumping his fists in front of the Arsenal fans celebrating in the Anfield Road end, and beating his hand on his chest. This was a vindication for him and his team. Five nights is a long time in football.

He had talked about the harsh realities of this sport after Tuesday’s loss. He had reminded everyone that playing at this level was not like ‘Disneyland’. And this victory was not like Disneyland, either. It was less a theme park and more an assault course. It was rough and it was unforgiving and Arsenal were equal to it.

Liverpool, improving under the management of Andoni Iraola, had been talked up as title contenders ahead of this match on a dank evening on Merseyside where the streets around the ground were decorated with the toothless grimaces of rotting pumpkins on doorsteps. The home team showed exhilarating signs of their re-emergence as an attacking force.

They dominated much of the game, too, but they looked like an emerging team, a team that is still evolving. Arsenal, marshalled imperiously by Declan Rice, looked like the finished article. They created one outstanding chance and Kai Havertz converted it. That was all they needed.

Their defence stayed rock-solid, although there was some puzzlement that Liverpool were not awarded a penalty for Jurrien Timber’s blatant shirt-pull on Alexander Isak. After the interval, Liverpool rarely looked like drawing level.

Kai Havertz gave the Gunners a lead to defend after finishing off a well worked move early on

The German slotted home after Declan Rice fizzed a dangerous ball across the six-yard box

Winning at Anfield was vindication for Mikel Arteta after Arsenal's defeat by Fleetwood Town

The opening had been predictably frenetic. Neither team forged a chance but Trey Nyoni, who has forced his way into the first team with a series of excellent performances in midfield, could have been booked twice inside the first quarter of an hour.

The initial infringement was a nasty tackle on Martin Odegaard inside the first minute where he planted his studs in Odegaard’s ankle. The second was a spiteful tackle on Kai Havertz. Neither received a yellow card, which gave yet more pause for thought about the red card shown to Dowman at Fleetwood, and its aftermath.

Let’s get one thing straight – the criticism of Arteta for his ‘treatment’ of Dowman was absurd. It has come to something when a manager giving a player a hard stare is interpreted by some as a disproportionate response.

Nobody is necessarily hankering after a return to the days of Sir Alex Ferguson’s hairdrier or Joe Kinnear’s rants that broke records for expletives but if a boss is attracting censure because he looked at a player a bit funny, we are in big trouble.

Arteta is not there to indulge Dowman. He is there to coach him and to teach him and to help him grow up in the context of a Premier League football club. His actions in Fleetwood on Tuesday fulfilled his obligations in all of those criteria.

Arsenal survived the initial frenzy here and took the lead after 16 minutes. Liverpool were the authors of their own downfall. They gave the ball away from a goal kick, it was worked to Noni Madueke on the right, and when Madueke fed it to Declan Rice on the overlap, Rice crossed beautifully for Havertz, who touched it home at the back post.

Arsenal nearly returned the favour a minute later when they played themselves into trouble at the back. Bradley Barcola found himself through on David Raya but his first touch let him down and Rice moved across to clear the danger.

Alexis Mac Allister was left with his head in his hands after missing a glorious chance to score

Liverpool's 19-year-old talent Trey Nyoni started the match but was replaced in the second half

Liverpool recovered and began to dominate the game. Barcola’s pace began to cause Arsenal all sorts of problems down their right flank and Liverpool came close to an equaliser when Virgil van Dijk flicked on a corner and Alexander Isak was denied by the brave intervention of Raya.

Arsenal were still threatening on the counter. Christos Tzolis chipped a ball to the back post and, as Liverpool scrambled to clear it, Madueke turned it back across goal. The ball was intended for Havertz, who was unmarked in the middle, but Timber could not get out of the way of it and it bounced off him into touch.

The atmosphere was febrile. Liverpool had three appeals for penalties, first for Timber’s shirt pull on Isak, then for challenges on Alexis Mac Allister and Cody Gakpo, turned down in quick succession. Tempers began to flare on the benches.

The breathlessness of the match was relentless. Florian Wirtz drove a free kick against the face of the crossbar with Raya beaten and then, three minutes before the interval, Mac Allister ran on to a cross from Milos Kerkez and, with the goal at his mercy, directed his free header too high.

Liverpool laid siege to the Arsenal goal after the break but the openings just would not come. Isak blazed high over the bar from an angle, Wirtz had a shot on the turn blocked and then, just before the hour, Dominik Szoboszlai replaced Nyoni and, to more acclaim, Rio Ngumoha came on for Gakpo.

Still Liverpool could not prise Arsenal open. Arsenal began to grow in confidence and threat. The home team were grateful to Jeremy Jacquet for a clearance that prevented Odegaard turning Tzolis’s cross into an open goal, for Van Dijk’s brilliant interception to deny Havertz and, most of all, for a quite magnificent one-handed save from Alisson that diverted a Tzolis shot round the post. It will stand the test of time as one of the saves of the season.

Arsenal put in another excellent defensive display to frustrate and keep Liverpool at bay

Liverpool’s frustration boiled over. Mac Allister was booked for his part in an ugly fracas with Odegaard and Madueke. The stands became a mass of pointing fingers and shouts of protest and anger. Time-wasting and play-acting peppered the match. Liverpool felt the game slipping away in the angst.

Liverpool threw everything at it in the final minutes. Lewis Koumas flung himself at a bouncing ball but could not get enough power on his header, Ngumoha had a shot charged down, Barcola desperately searched for pockets of space but could not find them. There were six minutes of time added on but there was no way through. Arsenal’s defence would not yield.

#1547. Gabriel and Mac Allister's cheating is not just embarrassing, it's malevolent and wicked... players need the threat of red cards for such dishonesty and - if that fails - punishments after review, writes IAN LADYMAN

Published: 18:05 EDT, 1 November 2026 | Updated: 06:37 EDT, 2 November 2026

Football’s lawmakers like to meddle. The problem is they do it in areas that tend not to need any meddling. Like around handball and offside and other places that were doing just fine as they were.

So here’s a tip for the meddlers at the International Football Association Board. Meddle somewhere that needs it. Meddle in a way that would be meaningful and important and in a way that would actually help the game.

Please meddle with cheating. Please do something that would spare us from the embarrassment of grown men behaving like children in a bid to get other players booked and sent off. Yes, please meddle there.

Because football at the top level really needs it.

It needs a route through which players such as Alexis Mac Allister and Gabriel Magalhaes can be properly punished, shamed and embarrassed for what they did during Sunday’s otherwise fabulous Premier League game between Liverpool and Arsenal at Anfield.

It needs a deterrent. It needs greater power to match referees and greater leeway for retrospective punishment.

Alexis Mac Allister drops to the floor holding his face after his forehead is slightly brushed

The Liverpool man tried to get Noni Madueke sent off during Arsenal's 1-0 victory at Anfield

In a way, it is handy that there was one from each team this time. That way, we can be spared the usual accusations of bias that tend to come when footballers are called out for their sins.

Here, live on TV, Gabriel and Mac Allister were both as bad as each other. One in each half, clear as day.

Arsenal defender Gabriel was poked in the chest early on by Aleksandar Isak and went down holding his face. Then, much later, Liverpool’s Mac Allister was brushed by the forehead of Noni Madueke and did likewise.

Neither fooled referee Andy Madley. Both were told to get up and get on with the game. On TV, Sky Sports analysts Gary Neville and Jamie Carragher didn’t hold back.

‘Embarrassing’ was the word they both chose. Neville to describe Gabriel and Carragher as a way of calling out Mac Allister.

But this type of chicanery is more than that. We see it from lots of players and we see it all the time. It’s not just embarrassing. It goes much deeper. It’s malevolent. It’s low. It’s pre-meditated. It’s wicked.

Short of dark subjects such as spitting and leg-breaking tackles, I can’t think of much worse things on a football field than pretending to have a head or facial injury when you actually haven’t.

So where IFAB need to get involved – where they need to ‘meddle’ – is simple. They must increase football’s powers to punish.

On the field and in the moment, referees can issue yellow cards for simulation and for cheating. Players can be booked for exaggerating contact (Mac Allister) or pretending contact has been made with a certain area of the body when it hasn’t (Gabriel).

Arsenal defender Gabriel Magalhaes performed a similar act of cheating in the first half

The Brazilian fell down clutching his face after Alexander Isak brushed his neck and chest

But why is there no power – at least in occasional and exceptional circumstances - to issue a red card?

Gabriel and Mac Allister appeared to be trying to get their opponents sent off. Would they do it if they knew the match referee at least had the option of showing them the red card instead?

Retrospectively, meanwhile, we need greater leeway for action.

Under a law passed a decade ago, a player can theoretically be banned by a review panel for two-games for ‘successful deception of a match official’. However the reality is that the initiative has largely been superseded by VAR and was only really used for players diving to try and win penalties anyway.

In terms of the nonsense we witnessed at Anfield on Sunday – and indeed see on a reasonably regular basis around the country – there is very little recourse once the game is over so once again a possible deterrent has been removed from the equation.

Cheating of this nature currently looks and feels like a risk worth taking and that is what must change.

Alexander Isak was not given a penalty despite being blatantly pulled back by Jurrien Timber

Here, it was interesting to hear Liverpool manager Andoni Iraola suggest afterwards that he must start telling his players to go down under contact. He was talking about Isak’s refusal to buckle under a clear penalty area shirt tug from Jurrien Timber.

That’s an important issue, too. Players should not be punished for their honesty. A foul is a foul, regardless of the reaction. VAR should have awarded a penalty.

But here on an otherwise fine day for the Premier League, another known and rather ugly blot on the landscape grew larger.

The threat of red cards for cheating and – if that fails - punishments handed down by review. That’s the kind of meddling we should all be on board with.

#1546. Same old Spurs given reality check of epic proportions

The players and the transfer fees might be different, but this was same old Tottenham Hotspur. The same Tottenham that finished each of the last two seasons in 17th. The same Tottenham that folded in adversity. The same Tottenham that opposition fans loved to laugh at.

Of course, it is very early days and the good news for Spurs fans and head coach Roberto De Zerbi is the side that started the opening day humiliation to Brentford may well never play together again this season.

But in a summer in which Tottenham have allowed their fans to dream of good times ahead by breaking the bank in the transfer window, this was a reality check of epic proportions.

The Spurs supporters who have become sick of being made the butt of their rivals’ jokes had to listen to Brentford fans singing “Thomas Frank, he’s laughing at you” in reference to the Dane’s unhappy spell in north London.

The impending arrival of Savinho will take Tottenham’s spending over £300m, but none of their big-money debutants at the Gtech Community Stadium hit the ground running.

There was only one man who looked anything close to a £100m player and it was not Sandro Tonali.

Tottenham’s first-ever £100m signing was completely upstaged by Brentford’s Mamadou Sangaré on his first competitive start for the club, as Spurs were run ragged.

Sangaré might not have scored on his Brentford debut, but he had a major contribution in two of his side’s goals and bossed the middle of the park. He deservedly received a standing ovation when he was substituted with 15 minutes remaining.

“He is a top player, no doubt about it,” said head coach Keith Andrews. “He is the one we were after in the window. The club deserve a lot of credit because a lot of clubs were looking at him.

“He deserves a lot of credit too, because he could have gone elsewhere for a few more bob. He recognised this would be a good place to come and he has settled quite nicely.”

A club-record £39m signing from French club Lens, Sangaré may prove to be a steal for Brentford. He ran the game for long periods and was responsible for Keane Lewis-Potter’s opening goal.

Having played a lovely one-two with Dango Ouattara, Sangaré kept his cool to brilliantly pick out Lewis-Potter and give him the easy task of finding the back of the net.

Keane Lewis-Potter scores Brentford's first goal of the new season!Brilliant play from record signing Mamadou Sangaré 👏 pic.twitter.com/Ua9HklQaWh

Later in the first half, Sangaré won a free-kick in his own half thanks to some quick feet and the action produced a big cheer from the home fans.

Tonali was the subject of chants of “what a waste of money” from Brentford supporters. It was a volley that sailed high over the crossbar that prompted that particular song, but Tonali was not just off target with his shooting.

He lost possession on a couple of occasions at both ends of the pitch and allowed Brentford players to glide past him during the opening stages of the match. He struggled to get around the pitch and Tottenham generally lacked desire and fight – two things that clubs cannot buy.

Richarlison, Lucas Bergvall and goalkeeper Antonin Kinsky can all be disappointed with Brentford’s second goal. Richarlison’s hold-up play was terrible, Bergvall produced a weak challenge that allowed Mathias Jensen to take the ball and shoot, and Kinsky parried the ball straight into the path of Vitaly Janelt, who scored.

Kinsky has been trusted to take over from Guglielmo Vicario as Tottenham’s number one this season, but this was not a good start.

Vitaly Janelt doubles Brentford's lead! 🐝 pic.twitter.com/AYh5BGhJBQ

De Zerbi spent much of the first half telling his back four to get higher up the pitch and it was perhaps understandable that captain for the day Archie Gray, Jan Paul van Hecke, Marcos Senesi and Andy Robertson looked like a group of strangers.

This was the foursome’s first competitive game together, but De Zerbi will need his Tottenham players to get to know each other as fast as possible if they are to challenge for Europe this season or even finish in the top half of the table.

Bergvall and Conor Gallagher were hooked at half-time, with Tottenham two goals behind and De Zerbi clearly unimpressed. But the Italian’s changes did not prompt an instant response. In fact, things got even worse.

Once again, Sangaré was heavily involved. He produced a well-hit shot that Kinsky had to save. For the second time, the goalkeeper failed to push the ball out of trouble and Michael Kayode was able to score.

Michael Kayode with a third for Brentford just three minutes into the second half! ⚡️ pic.twitter.com/40kOIlV5MU

De Zerbi can console himself with the fact his Spurs team will quickly look a lot different. There are more new faces to come in, with winger Savinho on the brink of joining and Tottenham hoping Omar Marmoush will follow him from Manchester City.

Mikey Moore, who forced Brentford goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher into two second-half saves, is expected to join Cologne on loan and Mohammed Kudus is close to returning from injury, while Micky van de Ven and Pedro Porro will come back in.

But if ever there was proof that spending a fortune offers no guarantee of happiness, then this was it.

Roberto De Zerbi has admitted that big-spending Tottenham Hotspur “are not a team yet” after watching his new-look side fall to an opening-day defeat to Brentford.

Tottenham have splashed out over £200m on new players, but head coach De Zerbi has warned it will be impossible to set any targets until they become a team.

Record £100m signing Sandro Tonali made his competitive debut for Tottenham, along with fellow new signings Jan Paul van Hecke, Marcos Senesi, Mateus Fernandes and Andy Robertson.

Tottenham have been tipped to challenge for European qualification, having finished 17th in each of the last two seasons, but De Zerbi acknowledged those optimistic predictions may have come too soon.

His team looked like strangers in their humiliating loss at Brentford and the Italian said: “We are not a team yet for a lot of reasons. We can fix the target [for the season] when you become a team. Before you become a team, you can’t say what you can do.

“You can’t become a team from the transfer market on paper. You become a team when the players find a connection, a spirit, a soul.

“We are not at the right point in our physical condition for a lot of reasons. Late from the World Cup and because in Australia [on pre-season], we don’t work in the right way. But no excuses, it’s a normal situation when you are building a new project. I don’t want time but we have to pass through these problems.

“I am surprised by the result and performance. They [Brentford] deserved to win and we played very bad. I knew we were not in the right condition. We can’t find an excuse. I am sorry for the result and performance.

“Marcos Senesi, Jan Paul van Hecke and Sandro Tonali are not in the best physical condition. We knew that before the game. We have to improve on that and many other things, like organisation and pressing.

“We can improve quickly but first, we have to understand this game better. I know their physical condition and [they are] new players but we have to put something more.

“We had to fight more. Players know I have a lot of confidence in them and we hope to improve quickly. Until we reach these conditions we have to suffer and today is an important defeat. Maybe we can wake up stronger.”

We had some problems with the timing of the pressure, we arrived too often late. We lost too many duels to compete with Brentford. I am sorry for that and sorry for the defeat. We have to improve in the physical condition and the organisation.

It was the first game and part of our journey, we knew we had a lot of new players. To become a team I said before the game we need two things, soul and style of play. We didn’t fight in the right way. Brentford is maybe one of the most important teams in the Premier League in terms of duels.

It was a game, especially in the first half, in one direction. We were not in the right position to make the high pressure, with Mikey Moore on the left centre.

We didn’t play well, we didn’t play in the right way. I think not because we don’t remember last season, because these players are good people but we lost too many duels. One of the best qualities of Brentford is the one-to-one, the man-to-man and the set-pieces.

Really pleased. Felt like there was a performance coming, you never really know after pre-season. The reality is the first game of the season comes and it can quickly come unstuck. I felt good for a number of weeks about how we were coming together. I was pretty pleased.

Our fans were amazing today. There is a genuine connection here that helps. I thought we started the game brilliantly and they were fully engaged. We want to be relentless. We looked like a real team.

That’s what we wanted, we wanted to start sharp, we want to show people what we’re made of and we did that today. We know last season we were one point off, this year, we’ve added quality people to the squad.

He’s been unbelievable, I can’t praise him high enough. He’s one of them players that we might lose the ball you just know he is going to win it back and he gets us on the counter-attack so quickly.

Seventeen-year-old Luca Williams-Barnett is one of the outstanding players in the country at his age group, and there is a lot of excitement about him at Spurs. Post-Kane, the club’s academy has not delivered much bona fide first-team quality, but Williams-Barnett appears on that trajectory.

Your Bees to kick-off the 26/27 season 🐝 pic.twitter.com/nJO5emjgQM

Spurs XI: Kinsky; Gray, Van Hecke, Senesi, Robertson; Gallagher, Tonali, Bergvall; Moore, Richarlison, Tel

Subs: Dubravka, Danso, Maddison, Udogie, Fernandes, Solanke, Bentancur, Davies, Williams-Barnett

Our Spurs side on the opening day 🤍🔢 @krakenfx pic.twitter.com/Uh5z221aTc

Starting the season in west London 📌 pic.twitter.com/uglTu9zDvA

Former managers Mauricio Pochettino, José Mourinho, Antonio Conte and Ange Postecoglou will all be scratching their heads about Spurs’ change of strategy in the club’s first post-Levy summer.

It was Postecoglou who publicly shared his belief that Spurs would never spend £100m on a player and yet, just over a year after his departure, the club splashed out exactly that on midfielder Tonali.

Whereas Postecoglou and his predecessors often had to answer questions over Spurs’ perceived profligacy, De Zerbi has been able to tease fans with promises of “bomba” signings.

Good evening and welcome to our live coverage of Brentford vs Tottenham Hotspur in the Premier League, a London derby between the smart spenders and the big spenders.

That is probably an unfair dichotomy, because Spurs’s squad has been crying out for investment, and that has certainly arrived this summer. The club’s new leadership team has overseen more than £300m worth of purchases.

The arrival of Jean Paul van Hecke and Marcos Senesi, two of the league’s best progressive passers from centre-back, makes it clear that improving Spurs’s build up play is a priority for Roberto De Zerbi.

De Zerbi wants his teams to draw pressure from opponents and progress down the middle of the pitch with short passes, so it was imperative that Spurs upgraded in midfield. They have done just that by buying Mateus Fernandes and Sandro Tonali, for a combined £185m.

Spurs’s forward options remain much the same though, which could prove a drag in the season’s early weeks. Compared to Manchester United, Chelsea, and Liverpool, Spurs do not have the same firepower, but they should have more control and solidity this season.

Brentford lost just three league games at home last season, and they were unfortunate not to qualify for Europe. A lighter workload offers Keith Andrews the chance to consolidate on an excellent first season as head coach, and perhaps overtake some of those clubs with continental commitments.

Midfielder Mamadou Sangaré, signed for £39m from Lens, looks the pick of their summer business, tipped to be a £100m sale to one of the big boys (which is an unromantic perspective on the transfer, but very much Brentford’s model).

Asked about the Mali international, Andrews said: “He’s a very talented midfielder who can do lots of different aspects of that role.

“He’s a very focused, very determined and very ambitious young man. He’s very humble but equally as hungry to achieve impressive things. He’s certainly a player on an upward trajectory.”

Forwards Jadon Anthony and Callum Wilson are other arrivals, and Michael Kayode’s long throws will continue to be a serious weapon.

#1545. 'It's certainly possible': Erik ten Hag sticks the knife in on Man United and warns his old club they could get relegated after poor start to the season

By LUKE AUGUSTUS, ASSISTANT SPORTS EDITOR

Published: 06:26 EDT, 2 November 2026 | Updated: 06:41 EDT, 2 November 2026

Erik ten Hag has warned his former club Manchester United that they could get relegated this season as their dismal season shows no sign of improving currently.

The Red Devils languish outside the Premier League relegation zone only on goal difference, as they sit 17th with seven points from nine matches - two more than bottom side Sunderland.

United have staggeringly only won one match in the top-flight, a 5-2 win over Premier League new boys Ipswich Town, a Premier League low that is equalled with Sunderland and 19th-placed Nottingham Forest.

Their plight worsened on Saturday afternoon after a 2-0 defeat at Chelsea - which saw them endure a second-half collapse and see Lisandro Martinez sent off.

As a result, pressure is mounting on under-fire head coach Michael Carrick and one of his predecessors Ten Hag – who won the Carabao Cup and the FA Cup during his two-and-a-bit seasons at United - believes the Old Trafford outfit could be mired in a relegation battle in the months to come.

'In the Premier League it's certainly possible, because all the teams are simply strong,' he said on ESPN NL, when asked about United's possibility of relegation.

Erik ten Hag has warned Manchester United that they could get relegated this season

Their 2-0 loss at Chelsea on Saturday means they're 17th - two points above 20th Sunderland

'They're all strong squads, all good managers. If you end up on the wrong side once and you really get into that vicious circle, then it can become very difficult.'

#1543. RIATH AL-SAMARRAI: Here's what I've heard privately about Max Dowman that proves he will come out of Mikel Arteta scolding a stronger player - and why he'll have dealt with far worse already

Published: 22:00 EDT, 30 October 2026 | Updated: 06:47 EDT, 2 November 2026

Mikel Arteta didn’t require the hysteria of the past week to know a thing or two about dubious reactions. Before we get onto his reaction to Max Dowman’s reaction, or the wider reaction to those reactions, we might revisit something that happened in November 2010.

That’s a long journey into the past, but the episode tells us a little about Arteta’s feelings for opponents who took liberties with his shins. The abbreviated version: violence would be returned with spectacular amounts of interest.

The longer telling revolves around a match between Arteta’s Everton and West Brom. To rewatch some of the footage now, we would say Gonzalo Jara brought it upon himself after 58 minutes, when in a mad passage he elbowed Leighton Baines and then barged shoulder-first into Steven Pienaar in the same scramble for a loose ball.

The defining act came next – Arteta stepped in to retrieve possession, but was clattered by Jara with one of those nasty scissor-motion tackles that could break the standing leg. If that sounds familiar, it’s because the challenge was near-identical to the lunge by Fleetwood Town’s Harrison Neal that provoked Dowman on Tuesday night.

But Arteta didn’t kick Jara, as Dowman did Neal. No, he stomped on his leg. Twice, actually. And with venom in each.

Arsenal's 16-year-old Max Dowman gets an earful from his manager Mikel Arteta after the attacker was sent off on Tuesday night against Fleetwood

It was a frustrating night for Dowman who failed to live up to the excitement that surrounds him

Dowman was around 11 months old when this happened, so he’ll have no idea about all that. And besides, he’d probably be wise to avoid bringing it up. Aged 16, his sense of which battles to pick will be growing by the hour.

But Arteta was 28 when he turned vigilante against West Brom. And it wasn’t quite an isolated incident.

Seven months earlier, Morten Gamst Pedersen stepped on Arteta’s ankle in a game against Blackburn and the Spaniard didn’t like it. His response? He poked Pedersen in the eye and got a yellow.

So let’s offer a couple of conclusions at this point.

One is about Arteta – if he wishes to present himself as a poster boy for the zen state and self-control in football matches, then he might need to torch a few archives. The two yellow cards he has collected on the touchline this season would suggest his own journey to enlightenment is ongoing.

The second, more meaningful conclusion centres on the general theme that Dowman should have been preserved from a few chilly words and a colder stare from his manager.

In the aftermath of Arsenal’s defeat at Fleetwood, that peculiar stance has been propagated by Paul Merson and Gabby Agbonlahor, who were among the vocal cohort that bristled and recoiled at the sight of a young pro being sent to the dressing room without a cuddle. The backlash against Arteta almost sounded as if he had abdicated a duty of care. Of all the reactions in this saga, I found that the strangest.

When Arteta addressed the matter on Friday, his justification felt far closer to the mark: ‘You have to understand the context. We’re not in Disneyland, we’re in the Premier League.'

If Arteta wishes to present himself as a poster boy for the zen state and self-control in football matches, then he might wish to explain why he gets booked so often

Morten Gamst Pedersen is left reeling after a clash with Arteta in his Everton days. A few years later Arteta would poke Pedersen in the eye during a game at Ewood Park

A hypocrite on the subject of retaliations? Yes, we can go with that. Wrong in his handling of a young player who lost his cool? No. Definitely not.

At 16, we can say Dowman meets the legal definition of a child, and a bloody talented one at that, but he’s not a kid. Kids don’t get into the Arsenal first team. Kids wouldn’t survive the hothouse of a Premier League academy.

To understand why that might be, it is instructive to look back to an update on the Arsenal website from the summer. On June 4, as they do every year, they put out a few words to detail which of their Under 18s and Under 21s had not made the grade, which was a list that included the names of Harrison Dudziak, Seb Ferdinand, Cam’ron Ismail, Will Sweet and Josh Nichols.

As very good players, they were all in the Arsenal Under 19s squad in 2024, when Dowman, aged 14, became the youngest scorer in the UEFA Youth League's history against Atalanta.

Of the starting XI that day, only four remain at Arsenal, and the point is this – Dowman has lived through the brutalities of that whittling process every summer and he will have been friends with those who had their dreams ended.

He will have been hardened by their traumas and solidified by knowing what it takes to stay standing in that world.

In short, when we attempt to imagine his position, and wonder how a cold shoulder might feel to a Gen Z child in the Arsenal team, we do so without the relevant context.

Because Dowman was never in Disneyland. A Premier League academy, even an excellent and caring one like that at Arsenal, will inevitably be more like a trip to the Hunger Games. Dowman has been there since he was five, so let’s assume it will take more than a mildly disappointed manager to hurt his feelings.

An incensed Dowman grapples with the Fleetwood Town players just before being sent off on Tuesday night

Dowman has not appeared flustered while he has passed milestones at breakneck speed in his short career so far

Based on everything I’ve heard privately and publicly about Dowman, his reaction to the reaction chain will go the other way. He’s a tremendously promising player and has a strong mind with good people behind him – it’s why he has not been flustered by any of the milestones he has passed at breakneck speed.

The wobbles, like the one at Fleetwood and shortly before that with England Under 19s, are few. But they are also useful, based on the truism that we all learn more when things go wrong. Viewed through that lens, Arteta’s worst possible response would be to indulge a blip or pretend it never happened. As an excellent manager, he hasn’t done that.

It is too early to say how far Dowman will go in his career. Likewise, we have no idea if he will shape into the kind of player who jabs a finger into the occasional eye or plants studs in any thighs. His reaction to Neal on Tuesday was certainly at the Disney-end of that scale.

But Dowman’s chances of succeeding will only be increased by learning where the margins exist. As with a few other facets of his game, he is ahead of the curve.

A confession: I find the Kylian Mbappe ‘dictator’ memes funny. If you haven’t seen them, the gist is pretty simple – someone once decided that he carries himself like a dictator and subsequently imposed his head on the bodies and uniforms of a few notorious figures from history.

One of those was Chairman Mao Zedong and Mbappe’s own amusement at that fact is why he was forced onto the journey of 1,000 apologies this week.

In China, where it remains taboo to query Mao’s actions in any way, Mbappe has since had multiple sponsorships cancelled and a diplomatic row has swirled, with the upshot that a state-controlled broadcaster is now refusing to screen his matches.

The space here is too short to relitigate the deaths of millions of people under Mao’s reign, but Mbappe might have cause to wonder if he ever really needed Chinese money that badly.

#1542. Enzo Maresca tinkers his way to nervy Man City win

Few in elite sport have the luxury of managing their own endings as Pep Guardiola did at Manchester City, yet no one can ever fully control a beginning. Enzo Maresca’s City started their Premier League season with a win, in the end, but three points masked the scale of the job he faces.

The narrative focus has been the impossibility of filling the personality void Guardiola leaves at a club sculpted in his image. That macro reading overlooks the number of distinct issues with City that Maresca must fix. A new midfield has to be recruited then blooded, a jittery defence needs settling down, and Phil Foden clearly requires help to recover the form which made him Premier League player of the year as recently as 2024.

All of that can wait after this victory against Bournemouth, which quietened some of the alarms from last weekend’s 3-0 defeat by Arsenal in Cardiff. Josko Gvardiol scored an injury-time winner after City had trailed for most of the match, much of it a sloppy slog for the home side, who went behind in the 26th minute. The introduction of Rayan Cherki for Nico O’Reilly revived some familiar attacking effusiveness.

A lesser-spotted VAR-aided double celebration capped a tense but ultimately joyful day for Maresca. Marc Guéhi equalised from Cherki’s well-taken corner in the final minutes, then the expanded Etihad Stadium rapturously celebrated Gvardiol’s apparent winner, only to see it flagged offside. Video assistant Paul Howard intervened to show Gvardiol was onside from Cherki’s pass, before City’s fans, players and staff shouted twice as loud for twice as long to salute a morale-boosting victory.

Joško Gvardiol scores in stoppage time! 👊 pic.twitter.com/FrTrfIg3ur

“It’s the perfect day to be honest,” Maresca said, although he may wish to set his expectations slightly higher. The East Stand which faces the dugouts at the Etihad unfurled a banner before the game welcoming him back to Manchester after his spell as Guardiola’s assistant. “I was very pleased when the game started, to watch the banner at the other side, and I was pleased at the end because we gave them the joy of the three points.”

His team made a fluid and furious start to Premier League football, suffused with a desire to prove the Community Shield is just a jumped-up friendly. A newly streamlined short-haired Erling Haaland ran with impatience, Elliot Anderson was a sinewy presence in midfield, Foden pulled off a gorgeous flick which led to a shot by Rico Lewis, well saved by Djordje Petrovic.

Maresca’s selection was surprising, with six defenders in his XI, some deployed unexpectedly. Guéhi partnered Anderson in defensive midfield, while their England team-mate O’Reilly was often just behind Haaland in a No 10 role. There was an air of destiny about one O’Reilly run down the left flank in the first half, cruising to the byline and crossing presentably. Haaland was well positioned in the middle, but utterly fluffed his lines. Samson similes on standby, although perhaps he too was short of full match fitness during his early-season visit from the Philistines?

Momentum shifted after Haaland’s miss, and Bournemouth took the lead when an innocuous high ball flummoxed Abdukodir Khusanov and Rúben Dias. They both pursued it, neither could make decisive contact and it left Evanilson on the ball with space to manufacture an unmissable cross for Marcus Tavernier.

Marcus Tavernier fires Bournemouth ahead against Manchester City! 💥 pic.twitter.com/lSyNRfrTlc

Marco Rose, their new manager, is facing a similarly daunting task to Maresca in living up to a predecessor who led Bournemouth to their highest-ever league finish and European football. “How the game went, it was quite unlucky to lose,” he said. “We had two situations, one corner kick and one attacking when we defended too passive, and that’s why we lost.”

His team showed an appealing coiled-spring quality after weathering the early City onslaught. They have players of class with the ever lively Tavernier, new signing António Silva seamlessly replacing Marcos Senesi at centre-back and silky Alex Scott, the Guernsey Grealish, whose current standing has now overtaken the man who gave him his nickname.

They could not hang on here though, with Guéhi atoning for a free header planted wide with his day-saving equaliser. Cherki’s corner was nodded in from around the six-yard line then, with the game in the balance, the Frenchman provided another, thanks in part to the semi-automated gods smiling on Gvardiol and his new manager.

"That is an EXTRAORDINARY miss!" 🫣Marc Guehi misses a golden opportunity to equalise for Manchester City! pic.twitter.com/Jl96MMmQeP

No mistakes this time from Marc Guehi 😤 pic.twitter.com/xlCJXWUzz6

City will need more, especially in midfield. Anderson at his best can cover the ground and roles of two men, which is just as well as City await reinforcements. The incoming Ayyoub Bouaddi will help, but it is a big ask for an 18-year-old to fill a spot vacated by a Ballon d’Or winner. Maresca was asked after the match about finding a “new Rodri” and deadpanned “Marc Guéhi”, who played acceptably, but is probably not a long-term solution.

There was a jadedness at times from City, which is not a great way to start the season, although they will surely improve with a bolstered squad and fitness levels. Maresca said “four or five” of his players who returned late from the World Cup are still effectively in pre-season training, including Haaland and Anderson.

Of course City are not the finished article, what team are one game into a new season? While there is a vast gap from this performance to their best, it was still impressive to smuggle three points from zero with six minutes left to play. Guardiola’s influence will be hard to shake, but that need not be a negative.

Marc Guéhi: Central Midfield Edition pic.twitter.com/ViBZqOroB2

The Maresca era begins with the most dramatic of wins. City were trailing 1-0 at 84 minutes, but somehow managed to turn it around.

Up until then, Villa - even with this unusual understrength side - were much the better.

Lewis is in fact playing right-back, with Guehi into defensive midfield alongside Anderson. O’Reilly advanced of both, with Gvardiol at left-back. All quite fluid, though, as you would expect from modern City.

Brighton 1 Aston Villa 0 (OG Lindelof) A disaster at the back for Villa. Pau Torres looks to play out from near the by-line but instead picks out De Cuyper inside Villa’s box. The wide man does well to steady himself before getting a shot away, which ricochets off the post, back on to Lindelof and into the net.

City have started brightly. Here Haaland slips in Lewis, who is unmissable with his new bleached hair, but Petrovic pulls off a smart save.

Chance! Ayari gets his pocket picked inside his own half by a buzzing Barkley. Buendia has a sight of goal but he slides the ball inches wide.

He’s at it again moments later, but he sends a third effort at goal over the bar.

Villa have started the brighter of the two sides. McGinn spins a deep free-kick into the box, which is cleared out to Buendia on the edge of the box but his shot sails over.

A warm minute’s applause for the former Manchester City manager.

Brighton are in their customary blue and white home kits shooting left to right, with Villa in black.

That’s a “Welcome Back Enzo” banner slowly cascading down the East stand. Feel that the tifo department has missed a trick, because it would have been very amusing to use a picture of Pep Guardiola, and see if anyone noticed. That could actually be Guardiola for all I know, my facial recognition is dreadful. Getting all of the trite “don’t they look similar!” observations out of my system ahead of the September cut-off point.

The teams have emerged from the tunnel at the Amex and the Etihad...

When asked by Sky Sports whether Ollie Watkins’ omission from the match-day squad was a sign that his Villa career was over, Emery pursed his lips and stared back at the reporter for a few seconds before saying: “Silence.”

After being pressed on the subject, he added: “No, no, no. We are playing today here. It’s OK. We are not speaking about [Ollie].”

"Silence" 🤫An unusual response from Unai Emery 😅 pic.twitter.com/kWNZtQu3PA

On taking charge of his first match as City head coach, Enzo Maresca told Sky Sports: “It’s big emotion. It’s a very nice feeling, the first game at home in front of our fans, so hopefully we can give them the three points.”

When asked about Elliot Anderson and the void left by Rodri, he added: “I think Elliot [Anderson] has to be himself; a good player, he’s going to be even better, but he has to be himself. Again, for me, there are no players that they are the same player, they are all different.

“We are happy with Elliot, but for sure, as we know, Rodri is a big player but he’s already gone. So now the focus is on the ones that are here with us and the ones that will probably arrive.”

Brighton have spent around £100m this summer but of those only the Croatian centre-back, Luka Vušković, is in the starting XI to face Aston Villa. He cost £46m from Spurs. Brighton have, as ever, sold players with Jan-Paul Van Hecke the biggest price. The expectation is that Carlos Baleba will leave for Manchester United. He is not in the squad. The injured Yankuba Minteh would not have been involved today - but he is another likely departure. Player of the year Ferdi Kadioglu is missing with injury.

Pep Guardiola’s successor assessed the breadth of the challenge before him and offered a candid appraisal of how to replace the irreplaceable. “It would be silly to try and change it,” he said of Guardiola’s grand design.

Tito Vilanova was addressing the world’s media in Camp Nou. For Barcelona in 2012, read Manchester in 2026. Enzo Maresca would be wise to study the manual for standing on the shoulder of a giant.

Charged with maintaining the standards of a two-time Champions League-winning team many still consider the best ever, Vilanova’s big idea was effectively to leave the existing one alone, mastering the art of the subtle tweak.

Describing the transition as seamless barely does justice to the changeover; Vilanova’s Barcelona side won 23 of their first 25 La Liga matches, snatching back the title lost to Real Madrid in Guardiola’s farewell campaign. Tragically, the promise of further honours to build on sturdy foundations was realised by others as Vilanova died from cancer in 2014.

After a brief stint by Gerardo Martino, Luis Enrique gave the dream team of Lionel Messi, Andrés Iniesta and Sergio Busquets further La Liga titles and another Champions League win.

The so-called “impossible job” of being bound by the weight of the preceding genius, therefore, was no such thing.

The Villa team is missing six of the players who started the Europa League final against Freiburg on May 20. Four of them have left (Ezri Konsa, Morgan Rogers, Lucas Digne, Youri Tielemans) and Emi Martinez and Ollie Watkins might be leaving too - they are absent today. Belgian goalkeeper Marco Bizot starts and there is also a place for teenager George Hemmings. Emi Buendia in what looks like the central striker role. It is certainly a bracing opening day to the season for Unai Emery.

No sign of Watkins in what is an objectively underpowered Aston Villa line-up. There’s also no start for new signing Suzuki, with Emery preferring Bizot between the sticks. Academy graduate Hemmings makes his first Premier League start.

He did not have a pleasant afternoon in Cardiff last weekend, although that could be said for several City players. Some lingering doubts about his physicality, in a Premier League becoming ever more hands-on, but Enzo Maresca knows him from his time as an assistant here and clearly rates him. Wonder whether that sentiment will endure if (when) City buy some new midfielders in the coming weeks.

Haaland will make his 200th appearance for City this afternoon. Either Lewis or O’Reilly could be deployed alongside Anderson in central midfield.

Welcome to live coverage of Sunday afternoon’s 2pm Premier League kick-offs. Enzo Maresca faces the unenviable task of following Pep Guardiola’s decade of dominance at Manchester City and his reign begins in earnest with a visit from Bournemouth, who themselves are ushering in a new era after Marco Rose succeeded Andoni Iraola. A bruising 3-0 defeat in the Community Shield last weekend does not bode well for City’s hopes of closing the gap to Arsenal, but Maresca will be telling his charges that this afternoon is a fresh start: a new week and a new competition, plus Erling Haaland has a new haircut…

The Italian’s squad has been shorn of World Cup winner Rodri, who departed for Barcelona this week, and the spotlight will turn to £116m club-record signing Elliot Anderson who is expected to make his Premier League debut with City. Jérémy Doku is out for two to three weeks after suffering a calf injury, which could open the door for Jack Grealish, with City bereft of wide options. City will have their work cut out as Bournemouth, fresh off a historic sixth-place finish last season, look to extend their 18-match unbeaten run from the end of last season. The Cherries won three of their five pre-season matches, which included an eye-catching 10-1 victory over Serie A side Genoa.

Brighton and Hove Albion welcome Aston Villa to the Amex for their 2026-27 season opener having travelled 220 miles north of the Arctic Circle to play Norwegian side Tromso in their Europa Conference league play-off on Thursday. Fabian Hurzeler’s side face the defending Europa League champions without Carlos Baleba, who is on the brink of joining Manchester United, as well as injured wingers Kaoru Mitoma and Yankuba Minteh. While Unai Emery has lost key players in Morgan Rogers, Youri Tielemans, Ezri Konsa and Lucas Digne, the funds raised has gone towards seven signings, with Zion Suzuki, the Japan goalkeeper, in line to make his first start for Villa.
