#1477. Villa end goal drought to finally give Emery’s new era lift-off

Unai Emery is building Aston Villa 2.0 and this was a night when his new kids on the block produced clear signs of lift-off for the next chapter.

Emery always springs into life on European nights and his reconstructed team secured their first win and goals of the season to leave Villa’s 1,700 fans singing in the rain.

Ten summer signings have arrived during a summer of upheaval, which included plenty of high-profile departures after the club’s Europa League triumph in May.

Yet this was an evening that will have further energised Emery on his return to the Champions League.

Nicolas Jackson, Zion Suzuki and João Gomes embody this new Villa team and all stood out here in Bruges.

Record £65m signing Jackson’s fine individual goal proved to be the winner to settle a chaotic, absorbing contest with the Belgian Pro League champions.

Jackson adds a third for Aston Villa after Sommer comes rushing out of his box! 😱📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/HZ1x3BkfK0

Suzuki, the £30m replacement for Emiliano Martínez, has clear presence in goal and he is Villa’s version of former Manchester City goalkeeper Ederson with his wide array of passing.

Gomes was also industrious in midfield to recover from what was a nightmarish debut at Brighton, where he was sent off after 40 minutes.

Despite all the changes to this team, talismanic captain John McGinn remains essential to Villa. He became their all-time leading goalscorer in major European competitions with his 12th goal and led by example again, as he has done so many times.

McGinn strikes to put Villa ahead in Bruges! 💥📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/FJnuxSwYwo

There were also hints of a strong defensive partnership developing between Pau Torres and Victor Lindelof, following the sale of Ezri Konsa to Arsenal last month.

“Fantastic, fantastic,” purred Emery at one point in the second half from the technical area, and Villa’s season now appears up and running.

Emery said: “This was another step forward and I am so happy and thankful for this. The old players need to keep our standards high and show everyone this is the only way we can achieve the process and reach our targets.

“It’s very important to start the Champions League with three points and hopefully this will give us confidence for the league. We are improving and we must work hard – it is the only way.”

Although Emery has established a reputation as the Europa League king, winning that trophy five times, this competition has proved more difficult to master.

His best run was reaching the semi-finals in the 2021-22 season, when his Villarreal side lost to Liverpool.

It remains a tournament in which he is desperate to make an impression, with Villa returning to Champions League duty here for the first time since their thrilling encounter with Paris St-Germain in April 2025.

Only five of that starting XI from the second leg of the quarter-final remain and one of them, midfielder Amadou Onana, is out until next year after sustaining a serious knee injury at the World Cup with Belgium.

With European heavyweights Barcelona, PSG and Borussia Dortmund to come in the league phase, this always felt like a game Villa probably needed to win.

They had only managed one shot on target so far this season before arriving in this historic city, but scored three goals before half-time.

Their opener came against the run of play in the 11th minute, with McGinn casually finding the corner after a lung-bursting run from Torres. McGinn has overtaken former Villa striker Ollie Watkins at the top of the club’s continental goalscoring charts.

Brugge briefly wobbled but were level eight minutes later when Hugo Vetlesen swept home from 10 yards, capitalising on space in the penalty box.

Vetlesen draws Club Brugge level against Aston Villa! ⚡📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/4ZYwPcMHim

Villa were back in front less than 160 seconds later, with Gomes teeing up Emiliano Buendía for an easy finish. Gomes was released in the box by a clever backheel from Jackson.

Buendia restores Villa's lead just minutes after Club Brugge's equaliser, and Unai Emery is LOVING it! 🙌📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/h2WGkwkTI1

Two minutes before half-time Yann Sommer, Club Brugge’s new goalkeeper, then had a severe rush of blood to the head by racing from his goal to almost the halfway line in an attempt to intercept Torres’s long pass.

Jackson edged the ball past him and held off a defender to calmly slot into the empty net. He underlined in many moments why Emery has pursued him for so long, after the pair established a strong rapport at Villarreal.

Villa appeared relatively comfortable in the second half until Aaron Wan-Bissaka was judged to have handled a cross from Joaquin Seys, after referee Sandro Schärer was advised by VAR to review the incident on his TV monitor.

It was a simple decision and Nicolò Tresoldi put away the penalty to stir life back into the home supporters.

Club Brugge are back in it from the penalty spot after Wan-Bissaka's handball! 👀📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/pEanRJvimu

Villa defended resolutely as time began to tick away with Suzuki providing authority in goal. The first Japanese goalkeeper to play in the Champions League also produced a number of routine saves in a nervy finish.

This was a promising night for a new Villa era.

Full-time scenes in Bruges as Aston Villa get their Champions League campaign off to a winning start! 👏📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/nYwtiQ6Xs7

Villa are defending with six at the back as midfield and defence merge into one. There are seconds remaining as Suzuki punts the ball up field and there is the final whistle! Villa make a winning start to the 2026-27 Champions League.

Another cross from the right is met, this time, by Tresoldi, but his header has no bite and Suzuki gathers.

Torres heads another Siquet cross behind for a corner. Brugge load the box but none of their players are able to get a meaningful touch on the ball before Diakhon slips just as he looks to get a shot away from the left of the box.

Slightly less mature play from Gomes, though. He bundles Vermant over and earns a needless yellow card.

Really mature play by Hemmings. Looking to break away, he simply puts his body between man and ball, inviting the challenge and winning a foul.

Villa are working hard in their compact mid-block and Brugge are struggling to find a way through.

Leko sends on Vermant and Diakhon for Potts and Virgili.

Barkley is one lucky boy. Attempting to play out under pressure, the midfielder gives the ball straight to Virgili, who cannot sort out his feet before offloading to Tresoldi far too late. A big let-off for Villa.

Gomes goes close after driving through Brugge’s midfield. He really should, though, have played in a free McGinn at the back post. Moments later Bogarde fires another shot goalwards but Sommer gets to it.

Villa have wrestled control away from their opponents. McGinn’s teasing cross evades everyone and Alysson’s cross takes a deflection which goes behind for a corner which is not up to much.

Lee hauls down Hemmings which gives Villa the opportunity to slow the game down. McGinn flights a delivery in from the left but Brugge clear their lines.

The ball comes out to Alysson who jinks in from the right, tiptoeing through a crowd, desperate to get a shot away on his left foot, but Seys does well to track his man and smother the effort.

Vanakan and Velesen and replaced by Tsawa and Lemarechal.

Yet another dangerous Siquet cross rains in from the right and here it is taken off Tresoldi’s toes by the tip of Lindelof’s boot. The defender did brilliantly to clear his lines at full stretch.

Hemmings burst towards the by-line and his cross trickles across the face of goal. Alysson is waiting at the far post but Seys does well to shield the ball and win a free-kick.

Villa’s best chance at putting this game to bed will come on the counter. And here McGinn plays in Jackson whose one-vs-one effort is stopped by Sommer.

Virgili from the left, Siquet from the right. Threats are coming from both wings and Villa need to get their foot on the ball if they are to take the sting out of Brugge’s attack.

Instead they allow Vetlesen a yard of space and his long-range sighter stings the hands of Suzuki who turns behind for a corner.

Emery switches out Buendia, Kamara and Wan-Bissaka for Alysson, Barkley and Bogarde before the corner is taken, and Suzuki stops the eventual delivery on the line after the ball spun off the post!

Another Virgili cross threatens to carve Villa open but they just about clear their lines. Then it is Siquet who delivers, this time from the right, but his cross just evades Tresoldi and Mechele at the far post. The home fans are invested in this, they believe their side can grab an equaliser...

Villa have got their tails between their legs here. From a position of strength, they have allowed the momentum to swing in the hosts’ favour and it has been largely self-inflicted.

Maatsen has a chance to break free but cannot build a head of steam before he is stymied.

Club Brugge 2 Aston Villa 3 (Tresoldi pen) Suzuki dives to his right early and Tresoldi slides the ball into the opposite side of the net. Just the one goal in it now!

Club Brugge are back in it from the penalty spot after Wan-Bissaka's handball! 👀📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/pEanRJvimu

Brugge have averted their attention to their right hand side, Siquet and Forbs attacking in tandem. A dangerous cross from Forbs is met by Tresoldi but he cannot get the requisite contact on it. Seys collects the ball on the far side and fires a delivery into Wan-Bissaka and out for a corner. Replays show that it comes off the defenders hand ...and referee Scharer is sent to the screen. He wastes no time at the monitor and awards a spot kick!

Villa do appear pretty comfortable here, despite some frequent pressure from Club Brugge.

Pau Torres has been outstanding so far at the back for Unai Emery’s team.

This is also a night where Emery’s ‘new’ Villa are coming of age, with Nicolas Jackson, Zion Suzuki and Joao Gomes also impressive.

Virgili then darts in field from his starting perch on the left. Tresoldi backheels the ball back into his path but Virgili’s effort is snuffed out.

McGinn, sensing Virgili’s growing influence on the half, takes matters into his own hands and leaves one on the Spanish winger, Siquet’s free-kick from deep is aimed at Tresoldi but Suzuki is wise to it and sweeps up.

Brugge are just reminding Villa that they are still there. Virgili is at the heart of things again, combining with Vetlesen who works the ball out to Forbs whose cross is well held by Suzuki.

Villa then spring forward, Hemmings breaching the Brugge box, but Buendia’s eventual effort does not make it through a thicket of legs.

Brugge are building with a three-man backline, sending Siquet forward high and wide. They’ve had much of the ball in the opening stages of this half, which is probably part of Villa’s plan. Emery’s side have settled into an out-of-possession 4-4-2.

Vanakan is booked for simulation after going hitting the deck off a challenge from Gomes. There is a knowing smile on the Belgian midfielder’s face which suggests the referee’s convictions were correct.

We are back under way... Siquet replaces Sabbe at the interval.

Nicolas Jackson is off the mark for Aston Villa. He beat Yann Sommer to the ball, held off a defender and was left with the simplest of finishes to round off a fine first half for Villa. pic.twitter.com/gWx6kUTlOX

Unai Emery has the new kids on the block but this Aston Villa team are hangin’ tough.

This has been a pretty chaotic first-half on the return of the Champions League but Emery will be satisfied with what he has seen so far. It’s very much a case of step by step for his reshaped team, but they should see this game out now.

It’s been a shocking night for Club Brugge’s new goalkeeper Yann Sommer. He’s just had a serious rush of blood to the head and was punished by Nicolas Jackson, who had an easy task to score Villa’s third goal. Sommer has probably ended his team’s hopes of a result here.

Club Brugge 1 Aston Villa 3 (Jackson) A shocker from Brugge, but in particular Sommer. Jackson races on to a nothing punt over the top by Torres, and the situation appears under control with two defenders in the striker’s orbit, but Sommer comes steaming out and Jackson nudges the ball past him before sliding it home into a vacant net.

Jackson adds a third for Aston Villa after Sommer comes rushing out of his box! 😱📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/HZ1x3BkfK0

A sloppy Torres pass out from the back goes straight to Vetlesen who picks out Forbs first time. The winger unleashes an effort from range but Suzuki makes a smart stop.

There is a shout for a Villa handball as Virgili prods a cross on to Kamara’s body, but his arms are clearly by his side.

Villa are presented with a great opportunity to break but the pass in behind for Jackson to gallop on to does not have enough juice and the move breaks down. Jackson does have a sight at goal moments later, but he’s only able to poke the ball wide off a free-kick from the right.

A really sloppy piece bit of play from Vanakan who cedes possession to Jackson and he’s straight into Brugge’s backline. He releases the ball to McGinn but the midfielder’s looping cross is cleared. Brugge need to take better care with the detail on their passes.

Jackson escapes the clutches of his marker on the half-way line with a deft spin and he feeds McGinn whose shot is blocked. The ball is worked to Hemmings after Torres is afforded space once more and a block takes it behind for a corner. Villa go short but the routine comes to nothing.

Maatsen flashes a dangerous delivery across the face of goal but the ball bisects Jackson and Buendia precisely and Brugge are able to clear their lines.

Brugge have certainly not given up the ghost, still looking to work the ball out to Forbs and Virgili on the flanks. Sabbe overlaps down the right but his ball to Vetlesen is cut out and Villa attempt to spring a counter which is snuffed out by Mechele.

Villa midfielder Joao Gomes is having a productive evening as he aims to recover from that nightmare debut.

He was sent off after 40 minutes of his first Villa appearance in the excruciating 4-0 defeat at Brighton and Hove Albion.

Unai Emery is expecting big things from the Brazilian midfielder, who departed relegated Wolves for £38m in July.

Wan-Bissaka drives down the right as Villa look for a third, but his cross is overhit and goes off on the far side. The right intent, though.

Club Brugge 1 Aston Villa 2 (Buendia) Jackson holds up the ball expertly before slipping in Gomes. The midfielder bursts into the box, outwitting Vetlesen before cutting the ball back to an onrushing Buendia who clips the ball past Sommer with aplomb. A crazy couple of minutes!

Buendia restores Villa's lead just minutes after Club Brugge's equaliser, and Unai Emery is LOVING it! 🙌📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/h2WGkwkTI1

Club Brugge 1 Aston Villa 1 (Vetlesen) Brugge are getting a lot of joy down the flanks. This time it is Vetlesen who finds space down the right and he spears a cross into the box. The ball is worked out to the left where the dangerous Virgili sends the ball back into the area and there Vetlesen is to sweep home. The stadium erupts as the Belgian champions restore parity.

Vetlesen draws Club Brugge level against Aston Villa! ⚡📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/4ZYwPcMHim

The Jan Breydelstadion had been very noisy but that goal has completely changed the atmosphere.

It is now nervy in the stadium and the Brugge fans are already starting to boo some of their players.

Villa’s first goal of the season and no surprise it comes from their talisman John McGinn.

McGinn strikes to put Villa ahead in Bruges! 💥📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/FJnuxSwYwo

Close! Hemmings races on to a cutback but his effort trickles just wide of the post.

Goalkeeper Sommer is penalised for handling the ball outside of his box. He had gathered a corner and had stormed forward to set off an attack. He changes his mind mid-throw and attempts to re-catch the ball but ends up wandering outside of his allotted space. The resulting free-kick crashes straight into the wall.

Sommer with an accidental handball outside his area! 😳📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/fBbqPEYyUJ

Club Brugge 0 Aston Villa 1 (McGinn) Brugge will be really disappointed with that. Torres is afforded the freedom of Flanders as he strides up from his own half to the edge of the hosts’ box. He offloads the ball to McGinn on the right of the area and the Scotsman steadies himself before curling the ball into the far post, beyond Sommer.

It is that duo again, Virgili and Seys. They have responded to Wan-Bissaka’s advanced position and are trying to pin him back. Virgili cuts in on to his right foot and forces a save from Suzuki to get the home fans going.

Aston Villa are still establishing their identity with a new team but it has already become clear how much they will rely on goalkeeper Zion Suzuki,

The £30m signing from Parma possesses a wide passing range and much of Villa’s build-up play starts with the Japan international.

He is Villa’s very own version of Manchester City’s former pass master Ederson.

Much has been made of Suzuki’s distribution and he has already teased a couple of lovely flighted balls up-field. Villa’s defenders are more than happy to lure Brugge’s first line of pressure forward but have not yet been able to find an incisive line-breaking pass.

Seyes and Virgili combine down the left in Brugge’s best attack so far, but Torres is able to head behind for a corner, which is not up to much.

Wan-Bissaka has taken up a very aggressive position down Villa’s right and he earns a free-kick in a promising position. McGinn spins in a delivery which is only partially cleared but Maatsen’s effort from the edge of the box is smothered.

Villa get their foot on the ball from the get-go, circulating the ball around the back, before Suzuki launches a long ball up to Wan-Bissaka. The ball is worked to McGinn who feeds Buendia on the edge of the box but his effort flies just wide.

There is a minute’s silence for those affected by the floods in Nepal which is impeccably observed.

The players then retreat to their halves and Jackson gets us going!

Brugge and Villa emerge from the tunnel to the Champions League anthem... Here is this season’s introductory VT to whet the appetite.

The Champions League is back. #UCL pic.twitter.com/bsFGV69KMP

"This is a good test and challenge for us today." 💪Aston Villa boss Unai Emery looks ahead to their Champions League clash with Club Brugge.🎙️ @LiamMacdevitt | 📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max pic.twitter.com/h4NF1jmiW6

As the rain lashes down in Bruges, you get the sense that Villa will have to dig deep to get a result and breathe life into their season. Both teams thrive on attacking transitions and the surface-level moisture will encourage breakaway moves.

Sep 8: Club Brugge vs Aston VillaOct 14: Aston Villa vs Fenerbahçe Oct 21: Aston Villa vs Viking Nov 3: Barcelona vs Aston VillaNov 24: Galatasaray vs Aston Villa Dec 8: Aston Villa vs Paris St-Germain Jan 19: Aston Villa vs Borussia DortmundJan 27: Slavia Praha vs Aston Villa

Quite the evening, last time out at the Jan Breydel Stadium 💫 pic.twitter.com/NogGLLSMFU

Opta’s supercomputer has worked its magic again this season and placed Villa as the 10th favourites to lift the Champions League trophy. Back-to-back winners Paris St-Germain are only fifth. Here are the leading contenders before a ball has been kicked.

Agree? Leave your thoughts in the comments section beneath this live blog...

Aston Villa 2.0 is clearly a work in progress after so many high-profile exits and 10 new signings.

Unai Emery has warned that it will take time for his new team to click, but this is an opportunity to spark the season into life.

Behind the scenes, Villa are feeling very comfortable about so much upheaval and it is the presence of Emery in the technical area which provides them with so much optimism.

For a deeper dive into why patience will be needed, read more here.

Brugge have conceded just two goals in five league games this season, but their Pro League opponents have threatened against the Belgian champions’ right side, especially in attacking transitions. Kyriani Sabbe is the more adventurous of Brugge’s two full-backs and the space he vacates will be inviting to George Hemmings and Ian Maatsen.

Here are a couple of examples of Brugge’s vulnerability down their right:

Don-Angelo Konadu, Lommel’s centre-forward, drifts out to the left and takes on Lee Han-beom whose centre-back partner Brandon Mechele has committed too far forward. As such, the space between Lee and covering left-back Joaquin Seys is too big and Freddie Potts attempts to recover from midfield. Konadu earns himself a yard with a feint inside and his shot is well-saved by Yann Sommer.

In Brugge’s 2-1 defeat by Gent a week earlier, Leonardo Lopes punches in a pass into the left half-space for Monodu Sonko to latch on to and from there the inside forward draws a save from Sommer. Josué Vergara’s follow-up strikes the crossbar.

The Spaniard added a fifth Europa League title to his CV last season while also guiding Villa to a strong fourth-place finish in the Premier League. Emery was today announced as one of five nominees for France Football’s Men’s Coach of the Year award – one of the Ballon d’Or accolades.

Christos Tzolis enjoyed an outstanding season with Brugge in 2025-26, contributing 51 goal involvements in 52 matches. His haul earned him a £34m move to Arsenal, where he has continued in much the same vein, laying on three assists in four matches.

While Tzolis wears the No 17 at Arsenal, his former No 8 shirt at Brugge has been inherited by Englishman Freddie Potts, who made the move from West Ham to Belgium last month. Potts has made a strong start to the season, serving as Brugge’s midfield sentry and starting all five of the club’s matches thus far.

One player to keep an eye on for Club Brugge is midfielder Freddie Potts.

He was signed from West Ham last month for a significant fee and lifted the Europa Conference League trophy when David Moyes was in charge.

Also in the Brugge team is Carlos Forbs, the former Manchester City trainee who had a poor loan spell at Wolves a couple of seasons back.

Club Brugge Sommer; Sabbe, Lee, Mechele, Seys; Potts, Vanaken; Forbs, Vetlesen, Virgili; Tresoldi

Substitutes Audoor, Coulibaly, Diakhon, Jackers, Lemarechal, Mike, Siquet, Spileers, Tsawa, Vanden Driessche, Vasovic, Vermant

Aston Villa Suzuki; Wan-Bissaka, Lindelof, Torres, Maatsen; Kamara, Gomes; McGinn, Buendia, Hemmings; Jackson

Substitutes Abraham, Barkley, Bizot, Bogarde, Garnacho, Mbaye, Mings, Ruggeri, Wright, Alysson

One player who will have many memories of this stadium is Villa centre-back Tyrone Mings.

Who can forget that bewildering moment in November 2024 when Mings picked up the ball inside the penalty area?

Club Brugge are awarded a penalty after Tyrone Mings picks the ball up inside his own area 😳📺 @tntsports & @discoveryplusUK pic.twitter.com/wpAqjMW8pn

Everybody loves a redemption story and on his return a few months later he produced a brilliant individual performance which included an incredible goal-line clearance to save his team.

Mings is on the bench today. Matty Cash is out with a muscle issue so there is a first start for summer signing Aaron Wan-Bissaka.

Addressing the media in Monday’s pre-match press conference, Unai Emery was asked about the challenges of taking Aston Villa into another season in Europe with a significantly changed squad. He said: “To continue in this level, changing some players, key players, but those key players we changed this year as well before the last year we were changing – not like this year, because this year was more players than normal, but we are replacing them.

“We have the players with experience like here with Emiliano [Buendía] and they deserve to continue here trying take now more responsibility and try to give the players we have … Of course we have now new players with a lot of experience like Goretska for example, and we have some young players, they are coming from [big] clubs like Garnacho, Mbaye or Jackson. We must try to adapt them in our structure tactically and arrive [at that point] as fast as possible … We need time, I don’t know if we need time or not, it’s not for me something I’m thinking about, I am thinking about competing. To compete [in] each match.

“We started the Premier League, the first competition, as our objective at the end of the season, because through it we can achieve our objectives this year, and we’re progressing. Still not enough, because we are not getting good results. But [the match against Brugge] is a new test.”

The experienced Yann Sommer starts between the sticks, with in-form striker Nicolò Tresoldi leading the line. English midfielder Freddie Potts is one of Ivan Leko’s two pivots.

Our ground crew for tonight. 👥📃 pic.twitter.com/UB7FUi9ZDH

Emery makes three changes from the XI that started against Hull City. Wan-Bissaka comes in for Matty Cash who does not make the match-day squad. Joao Gomes is eligible to play despite being suspended in domestic competition while Pau Torres replaces Tyrone Mings.

How we start this evening to take on Club Brugge in the #UCL 👊 pic.twitter.com/d7ftzgnoIi

Aston Villa are back in the Champions League and in familiar territory with an unfamiliar team.

This will be their third match at the Jan BreydelStadion in less than two years but much has changed with the players that last competed here for Unai Emery.

Two of the goalscorers in the club’s last outing in Bruges were Leon Bailey and Marco Asensio, who are no longer at the club.

Of course, they are not the only players that have left and this is a new-look Emery team hoping for lift-off this season.

Villa are the Europa League winners but this could be a tricky evening against the Belgian Pro League champions.

Good evening and welcome to live coverage of Aston Villa’s Champions League opener against Club Brugge. Unai Emery’s side voyage across the Channel to face the Belgian champions having triumphed in last season’s Europa League and finished fourth in the Premier League. The Villa mothership has since sailed into choppy waters, though, with a raft of big-name sales preceding a run of two defeats and a draw in the league. An opening-weekend thrashing by Brighton and Hove Albion proved quite the storm for Emery’s new-look crew.

Morgan Rogers alighted for Chelsea in a deal worth £117m, a record fee for an English player, and goalkeeper Emiliano Martínez followed soon after, while Youri Tielemans moved to Manchester United. Ezri Konsa and Ollie Watkins completed the exodus of leading men with late-August moves to Arsenal and Al-Hilal respectively. To remedy the outgoings, Villa twice broke their transfer record this summer, pipping Newcastle United to the signing of Johan Manzambi (£59.5m) before landing Nicolas Jackson (£65m, including add-ons), and added Taylor Harwood-Bellis and Ibrahim Mbaye on deadline day. Whether they can hit the ground running remains to be seen, but Emery has a task on his hands aligning his new recruits before the scrutiny intensifies.

Although Villa swept aside Brugge 6-1 across two legs in the Champions League quarter-finals two seasons ago, here Blauw-Zwart (Blue-Black) represent a stern test having made the Jan Breydel Stadium a fortress in last year’s tournament. Their only home defeat in the league phase came against Arsenal, with a 3-3 draw against Barcelona backed up by 4-1 and 3-0 victories over Monaco and Marseille respectively. Belgium’s second-most decorated club have won seven of the last 11 league titles and know how to win matches. In Yann Sommer, Ivan Leko has one of world football’s most experienced goalkeepers, who kept the most clean sheets in the 2024-25 edition of the Champions League (seven). Captain Hans Vanakan, Brandon Mechele and Joaquin Seys were part of Rudi Garcia’s Belgium World Cup squad, and German striker Nicolò Tresoldi already has four goals in six matches this term. English midfielder Freddie Potts could also feature, having settled in nicely in West Flanders having moved from West Ham United during the summer.

The earlier 5.45pm kick-off time, means Villa, Brugge, LASK and AEK Athens have the opportunity to top the 36-team league …at least for a couple of hours.

#1476. Man United Confidential: Club on red alert to prevent repeat of shocking Roma violence, why football insiders doubt Unai Emery is right fit for Old Trafford and meet the 17-year-old lighting up Darren Fletcher's impressive youth team

By CHRIS WHEELER, NORTHERN SPORTS WRITER and NATHAN SALT - FOOTBALL REPORTER

Published: 09:07 EDT, 3 November 2026 | Updated: 09:16 EDT, 3 November 2026

Manchester United are on high alert to prevent Roma fans infiltrating the areas of Old Trafford reserved for home supporters in tonight’s Champions League clash.

The fixture has a history of violence and United are determined to make sure more trouble isn’t sparked by Italian ultras buying tickets in the United sections of the stadium.

There were flashpoints when Galatasaray visited Old Trafford in October 2023, and again when Rangers were in town last year after tickets fell into the wrong hands.

There were concerns that the risk of unrest might be heightened by tickets for recent United games going on general sale, but the club insist they are only allocated to fans who were on their database prior to the Champions League draw being made.

The same restrictions apply to supporters forwarding season tickets and all hospitality guests whose tickets have been checked individually before being issued.

However, United will be extra vigilant to prevent Roma fans ending up among the home supporters, with any stray travelling fans being ejected immediately.

The rivalry between United and Roma dates back to their first meeting in April 2007 when Italian riot police were widely criticised for wading into English fans

United won the return leg of the quarter-final 7-1, with police making 18 arrests after fans clashed outside Old Trafford

The official allocation for the Italian club is 3,300, and those fans will congregate at Shambles Square in the city centre before making their way to Old Trafford under close police supervision.

Confidential understands Roma have avoided trouble playing away in Serie A and Europe this season after the Italian football authorities restricted travel for most of their teams.

With the exception of their games against Como and Udinese, Roma have only been allowed to take fans who live outside the Lazio region and are more likely to be affiliated to official fan clubs than the hardcore ultras who live in the centre of Rome.

The rivalry between United and Roma dates back to their first meeting in the quarter-final of the Champions League in April 2007 when Italian riot police were widely criticised for wading into English fans after they reacted to being pelted with missiles by Roma supporters.

A number of United fans were hospitalised, including 10 who were stabbed after being ambushed outside the Stadio Olimpico before kick-off. Roma were fined £31,000 – twice as much as United – and The Independent Manchester United Supporters’ Association pursued legal action against the Italian police for years afterwards.

United won the return leg 7-1, with police making 18 arrests after fans clashed outside Old Trafford. Sir Alex Ferguson’s side knocked Roma out of the quarter-finals again the following season on their way to winning the Champions League, having also played each other in the group stage – when trouble flared in Rome and three fans were stabbed.

Wayne Rooney scores United's third goal in that 7-1 thrashing. Michael Carrick also got on the scoresheet twice

The most recent meeting between the two clubs, in the Europa League semi-final in 2021, was played behind closed doors due to Covid.

A GMP spokesperson said: 'Greater Manchester Police is expecting a number of Roma supporters arriving into Manchester today with officers at the airport and would like to offer a warm welcome to all supporters.

'We are highly experienced in policing high-profile events and have been working closely with both clubs and supporters to ensure everyone can enjoy the match safely. We understand the majority of supporters attend matches peacefully however if there are any issues of disorder, we have a full plan in place to deal with concerns and will take action appropriately.

'There will be police in and around Old Trafford, so if you have any concerns before, during or after the match, then please speak to officers or stewards.'

The United squad flew back from London after Saturday’s defeat by Chelsea, avoiding the rail chaos that piled more misery onto their suffering fans.

Michael Carrick and the players took the train from Stockport to Euston on Friday, but returned by plane following the 2-0 loss. They were back at Carrington and heading for home by the time many supporters were left stranded by widespread delays caused by a points failure at Camden.

Confidential understands only one train left Euston for Manchester on Saturday evening and that was rammed with passengers desperate to get home and avoid having to pay for a hotel stay.

British Transport Police had to intervene to calm several disturbances before the train left Euston after standing still on the platform for half an hour, finally arriving at Manchester Piccadilly well after midnight.

Carrick and his players had a miserable time at Stamford Bridge on Saturday - but they did at least avoid the train chaos that affected the club's fans

When it comes to Ineos and the footballing decisions at United, much is made about the ‘best in class’ structure they have supposedly put in place.

There is Jason Wilcox as director of football, Christopher Vivell as director of recruitment, with figures like Michael Sansoni, director of data, key to the Ineos eco-system at Old Trafford. Omar Berrada is CEO and Sir Jim Ratcliffe is very hands-on as minority owner.

Carrick slotted into that set-up as head coach without ruffling any feathers. Should he get the boot, it’s fair to question if the structure is actually fit for purpose.

Chatting to Confidential in recent days, sources in the game explained why the current structure would not necessarily suit someone like Unai Emery.

As one of the best managers in the Premier League, Emery should be a dream target if United are to move on from Carrick in the coming weeks. He is, it is understood, on a five-man shortlist of potential replacements.

But Aston Villa boss Emery, for example, is said to choose his own sporting director and deal directly with ownership – rather than a director of football or a CEO – given the immense power he wields.

Would Unai Emery be happy to work with the likes of Omar Berrada (left) and Jason Wilcox?

There are serious questions being asked of Wilcox and Berrada right now. What happens moving forward with Vivell is also an issue.

Which raises the question: if United pivot in the dugout in a bid to save this sorry season and they have any chance of landing a big fish like Emery, why would you stick to a system that wouldn’t be agreeable to one of the league’s very best managers?

Maybe the structure is the problem, after all.

It’s approaching half a century since United’s famous win over Liverpool in the 1977 FA Cup final denied Bob Paisley’s side the chance of winning the Treble, but the rivalry has paid off for the family of Emlyn Hughes.

When the two clubs met again at Wembley later that summer and shared the Charity Shield after a goalless draw, Liverpool’s captain and No 6 swapped shirts with his United counterpart Martin Buchan whose white Admiral jersey with the three vertical stripes sold for £10,000 at auction on Monday.

The shirt, which had an estimate of between £4-6,000, was one of 200 lots from Hughes’ career with Liverpool, Wolves and England which were auctioned off by Budds on behalf of his family. A Northern Ireland No 8 jersey worn by George Best also sold for £49,000.

Hughes, who died in 2004 at the age of 57, led the great Liverpool side that would have beaten United by 22 years to become the first English club to win the league title, European Cup and FA Cup in the same season were it not for Tommy Docherty’s team, captained by Buchan, beating them 2-1.

Almost 50 years later, the rivalry between the two clubs is still as strong as ever as United prepare to go to Anfield straight after the international break.

Finding slivers of positivity at United right now is far from easy, but Darren Fletcher’s Under 18s are doing their level best as their 10-game unbeaten run goes on.

Spearheaded by Kai Rooney, Noah Ajayi and Jaume Camacho, Fletcher’s fledglings have hit 38 goals in the past 10 games, scoring 16 in the past three alone with a 6-3 win over Liverpool followed up by a 6-0 win at Burnley and a 4-1 win at Blackburn.

Jaume Camacho, 17, is a real rising star and helping Darren Fletcher's Under 18s play some scintillating football

This was a squad overshadowed by the brilliance of JJ Gabriel last season and one that started this campaign without too much star power on paper.

But with Camacho, 17, a real rising star – his four goals against Liverpool were sublime – Fletcher’s side are playing some top football and dismantling teams the way other clubs are dismantling United's first team right now.

United have 99 problems, but Fletcher’s Under 18s aren’t one.

#1475. Synergy in viral–bacterial co-infection expedites algal bloom demise

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

Algal bloom demise, often caused by viruses, is a major driver of carbon cycling in the surface ocean1,2. However, although blooms collapse synchronously, fewer than 30% of algal cells are actively infected by viruses3, indicating the involvement of additional mortality agents. Here we quantified tripartite interactions within a synthetic community composed of the abundant coccolithophore Gephyrocapsa huxleyi, bacteria and viruses isolated during a bloom. We found that bacteria significantly enhanced virus-induced algal mortality in G. huxleyi as well as in three other globally widespread microalgae. We quantified this interaction using two new metrics: the synergy index, which measures viral–bacterial interaction strength, and the benefit index, which assesses changes in bacterial fitness. We identified Alteromonas bacteria as drivers of viral–bacterial co-infection, with consistently high synergy index and benefit index. We found that during algal blooms, Alteromonas displayed high chemoattraction towards infected cell extracts, accumulated in aggregates derived from bloom demise, and increased in abundance during oceanic bloom collapse. Viral–bacterial synergy represents a previously unrecognized mortality agent that controls bloom termination, modulating the balance between the carbon-recycling viral shunt and the carbon-exporting viral shuttle pathways, which influence global carbon cycling4,5,6.

About 50 gigatons of carbon are fixed annually by marine phototrophs, feeding the entire microbial food web7,8,9. A substantial portion of this carbon fixation occurs during large-scale algal blooms1,10. Therefore, microbial processes that control cell fate in these blooms can have profound effects on marine carbon cycling11. Algal blooms are hotspots for diverse interactions and metabolic exchange with grazers, bacteria, fungi and viruses12,13. Marine viruses, the most abundant biological entities in the ocean, are major mortality agents, driving nutrient cycling globally and significantly impacting algal bloom demise2,14,15.

Viruses regulate the fate of carbon and other nutrients16 through two distinct ecosystem processes: the viral shunt4,5, which fuels the microbial food web by catalysing nutrient recycling in the surface ocean; and the viral shuttle5,6, which facilitates carbon export through enhanced aggregation of lysed cells and sinking of particulate organic matter in the oligotrophic ocean17 and during algal blooms18. Viral lysis of algal populations creates a distinct metabolic footprint19,20,21, which can promote the growth of adapted heterotrophs22, thereby altering microbial biodiversity23,24. Yet, how virus-induced shifts in microbial community composition influence algal cell fate—and thus global carbon cycling—remains poorly understood.

We selected G. huxleyi (previously known as Emiliania huxleyi) to study algae–virus–bacteria interactions owing to its ecological significance in marine ecosystems. This cosmopolitan unicellular eukaryotic alga forms extensive blooms, covering thousands of square kilometers25. It has a crucial role in global carbon and sulfur biogeochemical cycles due to its carbon fixation, its calcite exoskeleton production, and the release of sulfur volatiles such as dimethyl sulfide25,26,27. These blooms are often terminated following infection by a giant double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) virus, the Emiliania huxleyi virus (EhV)28. Despite the observed synchronized collapse of entire blooms29, quantification of active viral infection using single-cell approaches revealed a discrepancy: fewer than 30% of algal cells were infected by the virus during the bloom’s demise3,30. This suggests that additional mortality agents may act together with viral infection. Inspired by findings from the biomedical field demonstrating that viral–bacterial co-infections synergistically increase mortality31,32, we investigated the interplay between bacteria and viruses during algal bloom demise. Using a bacterial consortium isolated from natural algal blooms (Extended Data Fig. 1), we showed that bacteria can exacerbate virus-induced algal mortality, revealing a previously unrecognized tripartite interaction with potentially important implications for global biogeochemical cycles.

We sought to determine the role of bacteria as additional mortality agents during virus-induced algal bloom demise. We hypothesized that if bacteria that are naturally associated with an alga contribute to its mortality, then an antibiotic treatment would reduce the overall death rate during viral infection. To test this idea, we cultured a xenic strain of G. huxleyi isolated from a bloom induced during a mesocosm experiment near Bergen, Norway24. In the absence of viral infection, the xenic cultures subjected to the antibiotic treatment showed up to 1.2-fold higher algal growth (linear mixed-effects model, P < 10−4; Fig. 1a and Extended Data Fig. 2a), indicating that under normal growth conditions, bacteria naturally associated with G. huxleyi maintain a competitive relationship. Infection with EhV induced algal population decline from day 1 (Fig. 1a). However, when antibiotics were administered to reduce the abundance of the algal microbiome (Extended Data Fig. 2a), we observed reduced algal mortality, up to 19-fold, compared with cultures that were not treated with antibiotics (linear mixed-effects model, P < 0.05 from day 2; Fig. 1a). This difference suggests that the bacterial community may contribute significantly to algal mortality during viral infection, indicating a potential synergistic pathogenic interaction between viruses and bacteria. Analysis of bacterial abundance revealed that bacteria grew to 1.5-fold higher abundance in the virus-infected cultures compared with the uninfected condition (linear mixed-effects model, P < 10−4 from day 4; Fig. 1b). The differences in viral production between antibiotic-treated and untreated algal cultures were significant during the days of viral release, but the abundances leveled off resulting in similar total abundances (linear mixed-effects model, P > 0.05 on day 4 and day 6; Fig. 1c).

Dynamics of xenic alga–virus interactions for G. huxleyi (Gh) (a–c), P. globosa (Pg) (d), M. commoda (Mc) (e) and O. tauri (Ot) (f). a,d–f, Growth curves of uninfected and virus-infected xenic algal cultures with or without antibiotic (Ab) treatment. b, Bacterial abundances in uninfected and virus-infected G. huxleyi cultures. c, Viral abundances in antibiotics-treated and untreated G. huxleyi cultures. Statistical significance determined by a two-sided linear mixed-effects model, followed by Holm-adjusted pairwise comparisons per time point. Data are mean ± s.d. (n = 4 independent cultures for G. huxleyi and n = 3 for all other species). *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, ***P < 0.001, ****P < 0.0001; NS, not significant (P ≥ 0.05). Exact P values are provided in the Source data.

To determine the generality of our findings, we assessed whether such synergistic pathogenic interactions occur for other marine microalgae whose bloom demise is controlled by viral infections, namely Phaeocystis globosa, Micromonas commoda and Ostreococcus tauri33,34,35. The mortality of all three algae was significantly attenuated when treating virus-infected, xenic algal cultures with antibiotics (linear mixed-effects model, P < 10−4; Fig. 1d–f). These results demonstrate that viral–bacterial synergy leading to algal mortality is a widespread phenomenon among key marine algal species. Notably, antibiotic treatment did not reduce the mortality of O. tauri upon infection with a specialist virus (linear mixed-effects model, P > 0.05; Extended Data Fig. 2e), possibly owing to the rapid recovery of a resistant population. This exemplifies that the extent of viral–bacterial synergy may depend on various factors such as host susceptibility, viral infectivity and microbiome composition. We propose that bacteria and viruses kill synergistically, whereby viral infection creates favourable conditions for bacterial pathogenicity, accelerating algal mortality and fuelling bacterial growth. Thus, bacteria naturally associated with G. huxleyi and other cosmopolitan microalgae can expedite their bloom demise during viral infection.

We sought to disentangle the interactions between algae, viruses and bacteria during algal bloom demise. To this end, we developed a tripartite laboratory model system using algal, viral and bacterial strains that were isolated from an algal bloom (Extended Data Fig. 1). We isolated the bloom-associated microbiome (BAM) from the demise phase and determined its effect on G. huxleyi during viral infection.

We next reconstituted the tripartite system by exposing axenic G. huxleyi cultures to EhV with and without the BAM community, and observed an enhancement of algal mortality in the presence of bacteria (Fig. 2a). Although viral infection alone significantly reduced algal abundance compared with uninfected cultures, the addition of the BAM accelerated this decline, resulting in approximately fourfold lower algal cell densities after 7 days (linear mixed-effects model, P < 10−4; Fig. 2a). This recapitulated our observations in xenic G. huxleyi cultures (Fig. 1a), confirming that bacterial presence synergistically enhances virus-induced algal mortality.

a, Growth curves of axenic G. huxleyi under four conditions: uninfected, with BAM only, with EhV only and with both BAM and EhV. b, Bacterial abundances in cultures with and without viral infection. c, Viral production in axenic and BAM-inoculated cultures. d, Bacterial community composition of the inoculum (In.) and over time in uninfected (bottom blue line) and EhV-infected (bottom yellow line) cultures. Data are mean ± s.d. (n = 5 independent cultures). Exact P values are provided in the Source data. Statistical significance determined by a two-sided linear mixed-effects model, followed by Holm-adjusted pairwise comparisons per day.

Bacterial population dynamics revealed significant proliferation in the tripartite system compared with the bacteria-only treatment (Fig. 2b). Similar to xenic G. huxleyi cultures (Fig. 1b), bacterial abundances in the virus-infected cultures were more than threefold higher than in the uninfected cultures 7 days post-infection (linear mixed-effects model, P < 10−4 from day 2), suggesting that bacterial communities exploit metabolites that are released during viral infection.

By contrast, viral production remained similar between axenic and BAM-supplemented cultures (linear mixed-effects model, P > 0.05; Fig. 2c). Additionally, we quantified the effect of BAM supplementation on the fraction of virus-infected algal cells (Extended Data Fig. 3), enumerated at the single-cell level using single-molecule fluorescence in situ hybridization (smFISH)3, based on the expression of the viral major capsid protein (mcp) gene. During the lytic phase, up to 70% of algal cells were virus-infected independent of the presence or absence of BAM (linear mixed-effects model, P > 0.05; Extended Data Fig. 3d), proportions consistent with previous work with infected G. huxleyi cultures3. These findings suggest that the bacterial consortium augments algal death without affecting viral infection.

To identify whether specific bacteria are driving the synergy of this tripartite interaction, we characterized changes in microbial community composition during viral infection using 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing (Fig. 2d). The bacterial community changed reproducibly in all replicates during viral infection. Whereas the uninfected cultures maintained a stable community dominated by Marinomonas, a pronounced shift occurred in the virus-infected cultures by day 4, coinciding with algal decline. Notably, the relative abundances of Alteromonas and Olleya increased in the infected cultures, from approximately 2.1 ± 0.3% and 0.01 ± 0.01%, respectively, at the beginning of the experiment (day 1), to 20.2 ± 2.7% and 32.9 ± 4.4% by day 7, thereby dominating the bacterial community (Fig. 2d). Concurrently, Pseudoalteromonas and Yoonia-Loktanella increased in their relative abundances, whereas Marinomonas declined. These findings suggest that viral infection creates a distinct metabolic niche that selectively promotes specific bacterial taxa that are capable of exploiting virus-induced changes in algal metabolism or cell lysis products, as previously shown24,36.

To disentangle the microbial dynamics governing algal bloom demise, we developed two quantitative metrics that assess the contribution of individual bacterial taxa to virus-induced algal mortality, and the effect of viral infection of algal cells on bacterial fitness. The synergy index (SI) quantifies the decrease in the algal population during viral infection in the presence of bacteria compared to viral infection alone. The benefit index (BI) measures the growth advantage that bacteria gain during viral infection compared to their growth with uninfected algae.

To calculate the SI, we use the area under the algal growth curve during viral infection alone (AUCvirus) and during viral–bacterial co-infection (AUCtripartite). We selected area under the curve (AUC) as our metric because it provides a biologically meaningful measure of cumulative biomass change that captures complete temporal dynamics rather than single time points and offers robustness through multiple daily measurements. We calculated the difference between AUCvirus and AUCtripartite and normalized this value using AUCvirus, which is represented mathematically as SI (%) = (AUCvirus − AUCtripartite)/AUCvirus × 100% (Fig. 3a and Methods). Normalizing the differences in the AUC creates a dimensionless metric, enabling direct comparison across bacterial strains and experimental conditions regardless of baseline differences. A positive SI indicates that the bacterial presence reduces algal populations beyond the reduction caused by viruses alone, with higher values reflecting stronger effects (for example, SI = 10.0% means a 10% increase in tripartite-induced algal decline compared to mortality induced by viruses alone). The BAM had an SI of 22.2 ± 2.3%, which confirms the substantial effect of this bacterial community on the virus-induced demise of G. huxleyi (Fig. 3b).

a, Illustration of the SI calculation method, comparing growth curves of virus-infected alga with or without bacteria. b, Application of SI to assess the effect of the entire BAM community, showing significant enhancement of virus-induced mortality of G. huxleyi (SI = 22.2 ± 2.3%). c,d, Representative bacterial isolates from the BAM with contrasting SI values. A. stellipolaris (Ast) MB63 exhibits high (SI = 20.2 ± 2.7%) (c) whereas S. pontiacus (Sp) MB3 exhibits low (SI = 7.8 ± 2.7%) (d) synergistic killing. e, Illustration of the BI calculation, comparing bacterial growth curves in the presence of virus-infected or uninfected alga. f, Application of BI to the entire BAM community (BI = 259.8 ± 17.0%), indicating a substantial growth advantage during viral infection of G. huxleyi. g,h, Bacterial growth curves showing contrasting BI values. A. stellipolaris MB63 derives large benefit (BI = 112.4 ± 1.0%) from co-infection (g), whereas S. pontiacus MB3 shows no advantage (BI = −17.2 ± 3.0%) (h). Dashed lines mark limits for the area integration, excluding the first day which is below detection levels. i, SI and BI values for bacteria isolated directly from the BAM community (black outline) or a G. huxleyi bloom (no outline), revealing diverse ecological strategies. Asp, Alteromonas sp.; Hs, Hyphomonas sp.; Ms, Marinomonas sp.; Os, Olleya sp.; Rm, Roseovarius mucosus; Ss, Sulfitobacter sp. j, Classification of bacterial ecological strategies based on SI and BI values, identifying opportunistic pathogens, killers, consumers and agnostic bacteria (log10(BI) > 0). Data are mean ± s.e.m. (n = 3 independent cultures). Asterisks indicate P values for differences in the growth dynamics as obtained by repeated-measures two-way ANOVA (b–d,f–h); exact P values are provided in the Source data.

The BI quantifies the growth advantage bacteria derive from viral infection, calculated as BI (%) = (AUCtripartite − AUCbacteria)/AUCbacteria × 100%, where AUCbacteria represents the area under the bacterial growth curve with uninfected algae (Fig. 3e). The BAM community exhibited a high BI (259.8 ± 17.0%), indicating that viral infection of G. huxleyi creates a metabolically accessible niche that enhances bacterial proliferation almost fourfold (Fig. 3f).

To identify key contributors to this synergistic interaction, we examined the SI and BI for individual bacteria isolated from the BAM (Supplementary Data 1). Alteromonas stellipolaris MB63 exhibited a high SI (20.2 ± 2.7%), indicating that this species enhanced virus-induced algal population decline by about 20% (Fig. 3c). By contrast, Sulfitobacter pontiacus MB3 had a low, non-significant SI (7.8 ± 2.7%), suggesting that this species is not affecting algal death during viral infection (Fig. 3d). Correspondingly, A. stellipolaris MB63 exhibited a high BI (112.4 ± 1.0%), reflecting more than twofold growth enhancement during viral infection (Fig. 3g), whereas S. pontiacus MB3 showed a slight growth deficit during virus infection (BI = −17.2 ± 3.0%; Fig. 3h).

To expand the taxonomic range of our analysis, we tested a total of 12 bacteria isolated either directly from the BAM community or from the G. huxleyi bloom (Supplementary Data 1), and observed high variability in both metrics (SI range from 5.4% to 23.2% and BI range from −17.2% to 451.0%; Extended Data Figs. 4 and 5). The three Alteromonas strains tested (MB63, MB67 and MB68) consistently exhibited a large effect on algal population decline (SI range from 18.6% to 21.7%; Fig. 3i), while simultaneously deriving growth benefits from viral infection (BI range from 18.5% to 112.4%; Fig. 3i).

By mapping all bacterial isolates onto a coordinate system defined by their SI and BI values (the SI–BI phase space), we observed distinct phenotypes (Fig. 3j) and propose a framework comprising four ecological strategies: ‘opportunistic pathogens’ (high SI, high BI), exemplified by Alteromonas species, which both accelerate algal mortality and efficiently exploit the resulting metabolic niche; ‘consumers’ (low SI, high BI), such as Olleya sp. MB6, which derive substantial growth benefits from viral infection without contributing significantly to algal mortality; ‘killers’ (high SI, low BI), including Sulfitobacter sp. MB51, which enhance algal mortality but gain no growth advantage; and ‘agnostics’ (low SI, low BI), such as S. pontiacus MB3, which neither increase algal mortality nor derive substantial growth benefits from viral infection.

To determine whether synergistic bacteria directly affect the mortality of algal cells, we quantified the fraction of dying algal cells during tripartite interaction (Fig. 4a,b and Extended Data Fig. 3). Dying algal cells were identified as cells with compromised membranes using the DNA stain SYTOX Green (Fig. 4a), and were further differentiated by their chlorophyll autofluorescence as metabolically active (high chlorophyll autofluorescence) or metabolically impaired (low chlorophyll autofluorescence) cells (Fig. 4b). During viral infection, there was an accumulation of dying (SYTOX+) cells reaching up to 76.9 ± 2.4% of the algal population (on day 4; Fig. 4a). The addition of bacteria significantly reduced the percentage of dying algal cells (linear mixed-effects model, P < 10−4) reaching 21.0 ± 1.5% (on day 3; Fig. 4a), suggesting that bacteria selectively remove dying algae during viral infection. Bacteria selectively cleared low-chlorophyll cells versus high-chlorophyll cells. In the presence of bacteria, the percentage of SYTOX+ cells among all low-chlorophyll cells decreased from 54.0 ± 4.1% to 30.3 ± 3.0% on day 2 (linear mixed-effects model, P < 10−4; Fig. 4b), whereas the percentage of SYTOX+ cells among high-chlorophyll cells remained similar (linear mixed-effects model, P > 0.05; Fig. 4b). These findings show that bacteria preferentially remove metabolically impaired dying cells during virus-induced algal demise.

a, Total abundance (grey) and fraction (yellow or red) of membrane-compromised (SYTOX+) algal cells in axenic G. huxleyi cultures inoculated with EhV only (light grey, red) and with both EhV and the BAM community (dark grey, yellow). b, Fraction of SYTOX+ cells that are still metabolically active (high chlorophyll autofluorescence) or dead (low chlorophyll autofluorescence). Statistical significance determined by a two-sided linear mixed-effects model, followed by Holm-adjusted pairwise comparisons per time point. Exact P values are provided in the Source data. Data are mean ± s.d. (n = 4 independent cultures).

We sought to determine the metabolic basis for viral–bacterial synergy in algal killing. We focused on lipid metabolism since EhV infection profoundly remodels the lipidome of G. huxleyi, inducing triacylglycerol (TAG) production and accumulation of intracellular lipid bodies37. We thus sequenced and annotated the genomes of all bacterial isolates and correlated the SI of each one with the completeness (per cent of genes encoded in the KEGG pathway) of its fatty acid degradation (FAD) pathway. We found a significant positive correlation between SI and the FAD pathway completeness (Spearman’s ρ = 0.669, P = 0.017; Extended Data Fig. 6a and Supplementary Data 2). Detailed examination revealed that within the BAM consortium, the species with the highest SI values, all belonging to the genus Alteromonas, also encode the complete enzymatic machinery for TAG hydrolysis and subsequent fatty acid transmembranal transport and β-oxidation, including TAG lipase, fadL, fadD, fadE, fadB and fadA and their homologues (Extended Data Fig. 6b). By contrast, species with low SI values (for example, S. pontiacus MB3) showed several missing enzymes in the FAD pathway. Among bloom-associated bacterial isolates, only Alteromonas and Marinobacter strains encode these metabolic genes (Supplementary Data 2). Although this may be a phylogenetic trait that is not causally related to SI or BI, these genera were recently shown to selectively degrade algal lipids38. Most importantly, Alteromonas encodes a TAG lipase, an enzyme that releases free fatty acids from TAGs for cellular metabolism. This feature may be particularly advantageous during viral infection of G. huxleyi as EhV infection induces the release of extracellular vesicles that are enriched in TAGs39.

Having identified Alteromonas as having key roles in the viral–bacterial synergy during algal demise, we investigated the ecological importance of this genus during natural bloom succession. To this end, we tracked algal, viral and bacterial dynamics in a natural environment, measured daily during G. huxleyi bloom succession in a mesocosm experiment24. Following six days at low abundance (less than 5 × 105 cells per ml; pre-bloom phase), G. huxleyi showed a steady increase in cell numbers (days 7–14; bloom phase) and, upon viral infection (days 15–23; infection phase), its population collapsed (Fig. 5a).
