#1473. Newcastle scrape past Millwall to extend Jaissle’s unbeaten start

Joe Willock’s deft finish ensured Newcastle United survived a tough test against Millwall to keep their excellent run in the Carabao Cup intact.

This competition had been fruitful for Newcastle under former manager Eddie Howe and although this match was hard work – as well as hard to watch at times – his successor Matthias Jaissle guided them through a difficult trip to south-east London.

He called it “job done,” and that was pretty much all it was. “We needed patience on one hand, but also to be passionate and tough. We had the chance [to score] and took it,” he said.

Newcastle have reached the semi-finals of this competition three times in the last four years, but struggled to get any sort of tempo going against their Championship opponents.

You could argue the winning goal came against the run of play late in the second half, moments after Millwall substitute Taïryk Arconte had smashed a low shot against the post.

"Livramento had a NIGHTMARE, he's so lucky" 😨Millwall were INCHES away from taking the lead against Newcastle 🤏 pic.twitter.com/X26aiTL432

Given they were missing 13 players because of injury, this was a brave display from Alex Neil’s side. They frustrated Newcastle for more than an hour, nullifying their attack, to the point where Jaissle’s team looked as though they had run out of ideas.

That was until Lewis Hall combined with Matias Fernandez-Pardo down the left and his drilled cross found Willock who cleverly used the angle to pass the ball into the net. Willock has been rejuvenated under Jaissle. He looked certain to be sold this summer but is now starting regularly under a new manager in the number 10 role his system demands. It has been a nice redemption arc for the former Arsenal academy graduate.

Moments after Millwall hit the post, Joe Willock strikes to put Newcastle in front! ⚽️ pic.twitter.com/rSB8yV6NRO

The victory is all that matters and extends Jaissle’s unbeaten start to five games. Given he arrived just three weeks before the start of the season, that deserves praise even if it is obvious there is a lot of work to be done to improve their offensive play.

Playing in their lilac, or should that be Parma-violet, third kit for the first time, Newcastle looked off colour in the first half. Even though Jaissle named a strong team packed with experience of English cup ties, they struggled to overpower Millwall.

There were a few half-chances as Willock forced a save and Jacob Murphy fired over. There was a header missed from a corner by Sven Botman, which should have hit the target and Yoane Wissa also mistimed his jump after finding space for another header.

Millwall’s two centre-backs, Jake Cooper and Caleb Taylor were immense, flinging themselves in the way of every shot and clearing every loose ball that came into their vicinity. Given their injuries, this was a performance full of fight and defiance from the home side.

However, there was also an absence of quality in the final third from Newcastle, the same lack of cohesion and incision that was apparent at home to Bournemouth last weekend and in the first half away at Tottenham Hotspur.

It meant Millwall were happy to play for set-pieces close to the Newcastle box and Taylor got in front of his marker, flashing a header wide of the post.

That lacklustre first half meant Jaissle’s side had mustered just five shots on target in five halves of football since the 3-2 win over West Bromwich Albion in the previous round of the Carabao Cup.

Millwall started the second period like a side sensing Newcastle were vulnerable. A thunderbolt from Jenson Metcalfe, after the visitors had struggled to clear two crosses, almost gave them a spectacular lead.

Newcastle saw lots of the ball. Millwall were happy enough to let them have it given how little they were hurting them.

So much of Newcastle’s play was slow and cumbersome. Their set-piece delivery was also largely inept.

Neil’s side retained a threat and came so close to taking the lead when, not for the first time, a long ball forward caught the Newcastle defence out of shape and Tino Livramento’s mistake allowed Arconte to run clear and hit the post from a tight angle.

Well in, @Joewillock! 💪 pic.twitter.com/5a8G7lzD3H

Speaking after the game, Millwall manager Alex Neil said: “I’m very proud, I don’t think we deserved to lose that game.

“We had some good moments, and we got done by a bit of sucker punch at the end. But I’m very proud of the lads.”

As for their injury problems, he added: “I didn’t bring the teenagers on as a token gesture, I need to keep the first-team players fit. We’re really at bare bones.

But we beat Bolton at the weekend, got a couple of defeats before that but we started the season really well and once we get everybody back, we’ll be in good shape.”

With the first of the 16 teams through tonight, the draw won’t take place until most of the teams have played next week.

The draw will be shown on Sky Sports on Wednesday 16th Sept, after Manchester United play Brighton. Man City vs Norwich will be the only game outstanding then.

The third round had to be spread over two weeks as the nine Premier League sides in UEFA competitions entered the tournament in this round, as the same time as their Champions League and Europa League fixtures began. To avoid clubs facing clashes, the EFL split the fixtures across the two gameweeks.

Still got some more post-match to come for you, but we’ve got scores from all our matches tonight now:

From the Champions League, Man City held out against Porto to win 2-0.

“I think we had a lot of chances in the first half, and we went in a half-time saying we need to  take our chances, so I’m glad we came out in the second half and we did,” said Willock after the match.

“100% [the competition is important], we’ve won it before so it’s very important to us, but every game is important to us. Especially with a new coach and a lot of new players, we wanted to start the new season well. I think we started really well and we need to continue and this was a big game in keeping that momentum.”

"We said at half-time we NEED to take our chances"Lewis Hall and Joe Willock react to Newcastle's win over Millwall 🎙️ pic.twitter.com/NDF3laD8nT

Take a look at the match-winner from Joe Willock:

Moments after Millwall hit the post, Joe Willock strikes to put Newcastle in front! ⚽️ pic.twitter.com/rSB8yV6NRO

The goal came minutes after Millwall were inches away from taking the lead themselves, as Arconte was denied by the post:

"Livramento had a NIGHTMARE, he's so lucky" 😨Millwall were INCHES away from taking the lead against Newcastle 🤏 pic.twitter.com/X26aiTL432

We’ll be bringing you more from the post-match now.

Joe Willock has done enough for Newcastle to reach the fourth round and keep the travelling fans singing all the way back to the North-East.

It won’t go down in history as the greatest Carabao fixture, but Newcastle found a way to keep their momentum going and give Matthias Jaissle a win on his cup debut.

Newcastle aren’t taking any risks as Hornicek sends the ball long, and the players keep looking to send the ball down-field.

Seconds to go now. Marschall sends it long for one last effort, but it is cleared out of the box...

Willock has come off now for Newcastle’s own teenager, Sean Steur. A few more minutes and the man now on the bench with have done enough to send his side through to the next round.

We’re into the final minutes as Millwall are throwing everything at this.

Millwall are not out of this yet, as Neghli comes down the left side, twisting his way into the box past his defender – but having done the hard work, his shot flashes low across goal.

Some more changes, as Ramsey comes off for Newcastle, replaced by Lewis Miley.

A double change for the hosts as Dykes and Kelly come off for Regan Monty and Alfie Massey – the former just 15 years old.

Seconds later, another teenager takes to the pitch for Millwall as Osei-Tutu is replaced by 17-year-old Tristan Parkes.

Newcastle almost have another! From the sublime to the ridiculous, as Willock makes another run, this time down the left, and passes the ball onto the edge of the box where Elanga meets it in space. He lets it run, before taking his shot, but it is straight to Marschall.

Finally Newcastle have their breakthrough! They punish Millwall as Fernandez-Pardo feeds Hall on the left, who cuts inside and slips the ball across goal, finding Willock to redirect the ball to slot it home.

Marschall releases Arconte with a long ball and he turns Livramento to find huge amounts of space on the right side. He races into the box and takes a shot from close range, aiming for his near post, but is denied by the woodwork and the rebound hits the seated Hornicek. The keeper is lucky to not concede an own goal, as the ball bounces up and over his leg.

Issoufou again racing down the right side, before cutting inside and taking a shot with his left foot. Hall, who has been so crucial in the Newcastle attack, throws himself at the shot, and it flies high for Hornicek to collect.

Replays show that González, who Millwall players claimed had handled the ball earlier, leant down to clear with his shoulder.

Issoufou sends a great ball in for Millwall from the right side, but it is cleared by a Newcastle player, accompanied by cries for handball.

The game is opening up now as Newcastle make a run of their own, with Willock creating an opening for Elanga to take the ball to the edge of the box, before Taylor slides in to block his shot.

Millwall could absolutely win this with a smash-and-grab with less than 20 minutes to go. They are pushing for it but are lacking some attacking quality to finish the job.

From six shots they’ve had two on target, compared to Newcastle’s three on target from 20.

Fernandez-Pardo gets his first look at the ball, making a very quick run down across the centre of the field to the left side, but Osei-Tutu stays with him and takes him all the way to the back line before giving up a corner.

Elanga takes the corner, punched away by the keeper but no one goes to finish the job and Newcastle get another corner.

Metcalfe, who had his red card overturned this week, is the first player to go in the book for a mistimed challenge on Ramsey.

Just a reminder that there is no extra time, so if we’re all square after 90 minutes, it’s straight to a penalty shoot-out.

Willock gets the ball on the edge of the area and passes it on a quick turn to Barnes just inside the box, but there was not much on his shot and Marschall collects easily.

Double change now for Newcastle as Wissa and Murphy come off, replaced by Elanga and Fernandez-Pardo as Jaissle looks for pace. Schar is handed the armband.

Free kick for Newcastle, right on the corner of the box. Murphy takes, but it hits the wall 10 feet away, and bounces straight back to him. His cross into the box is headed out, and for all the opportunities Newcastle have created, they are yet to find the breakthrough.

We’ve also had a double change for Millwall as Esse and Lovelace have come off, replaced by Issoufou and Arconte.

What colour would you describe this Newcastle away shirt? They look like the sweets Purple Violet to me. Although would you call it an all Lilac number?

It’s the first time they have worn their third kit. Not sure whether I like it or not.  Shame The Den isn’t a sell out although I’m told tickets were priced at £31 and Millwall have a lot of injuries too.

Newcastle get another corner after a run from Willock. The delivery from Hall creates a good amount of confusion in the box and Marschall isn’t sure whether to stay on his line or come out to punch it away. From within the bodies, Wissa tries to get a shot off from close range but it bounces and the keeper easily collects.

González commits another foul, pulling down Esse, to give Millwall another free kick from 40 yards out.

The ball meets Taylor at the back post, but he meets it in the air and can’t quite direct it either into goal or back into the six-yard box, so it goes out for a Newcastle goal kick.

Another half chance for Millwall as Dykes feeds Kelly on the right side, who runs into the box and gets caught between passing the ball in and taking the shot, with the ball going high over the box.

Another great challenge from Osei-Tutu as Willock makes a run into the box, but is brought down by a well-timed tackle from the right-back.

The corner from Hall is better, but headed out and cleared.

Barnes again with space on the left side and he sends a ball fizzing low across the box to the far post but Neghli is able to lean on Murphy to stop him making contact.

Scramble for Newcastle as the ball is sent by Dykes to Neghli free at the far post, who puts the ball into a very dangerous area just in front of goal and everyone jumps on. Newcastle get to it first, managing to clear it from the goal mouth. It is cleared outside the box and it bounces to unmarked Metcalfe, who takes a thunderous shot, putting his laces through the ball but he is unable to keep it down and it goes over the bar.

Despite Alex Neil’s premonitions, no changes for Millwall at the break.

Right-back change for Newcastle, as Dedic comes off and Tino Livramento comes on.

The earlier kick-offs of the Carabao third round have just started their second periods, but here are the latest scores:

Aston Villa won their opening Champions League fixture 3-2 against Club Brugge, while Man City are still goalless against Porto, which you can follow with our live blog here

And that’s the last action of the half, as just one minute was added on and that was taken up by Newcastle’s corner.

Nothing separates the two sides at the half, thought the visitors have dominated in terms of possession and chances.

Millwall have held fast and will be happy to be finishing the half level. We may see some changes from them after the break.

The game is opening up before half-time, and Newcastle go again with Hall and Barnes. Osei-Tutu does well to wait before going in to block Barnes’s shot and send the ball behind for another Newcastle corner.

The delivery is once again poor, but Schar is pulled down inside the box by Taylor and is furious that nothing was given. There’s no VAR so there’s no review to consider – but looking at replays, Millwall were very lucky to get away with that foul.

Cooper makes a perfect pass down the left sideline, allowing Neghli to find space and forcing Newcastle to clear it away fo a Millwall corner.

The ball in is promising but Hornicek gets to it and punches it away, but the hosts keep the pressure on.

Baggott floats another ball across the box towards the right back post, but Hornicek easily collects the ball as Neghli can’t quite connect.

Newcastle moving the ball well again across midfield and it comes to Schar, who runs into space and gets a low shot away, around 40 yards out. It  takes a slight deflection on its way, going just wide of the post.

González is not having his best night and makes a silly foul against Dykes on the sideline, giving the hosts another set piece. The swinging ball in is not nearly as good as last time, and only reaches the first man, Newcastle’s Ramsey.

Millwall get a free kick, and the delivery is good, allowing Taylor to connect on the header inside the box. He beats Hornicek but the header rolls just wide of the post, to the groans of the home fans.

Hall goes short with the corner and Dedic has lots of time to cross the ball in from the right. It’s headed away but Millwall can’t break on the counter.

That sums up the game pretty well: not much finishing quality from Newcastle but Millwall not creating much from their limited spells of possession.

Newcastle pushing again. Another ball pulled back by Barnes finds Ramsey at the top of the box, and his ball in connects with Wissa. Newcastle’s captain can’t head it in the right direction though and Millwall survive again.

The spell of pressure results in another corner for the visitors – and now we’re getting some pushing in the six-yard box.

I think Millwall have done well. They have limited Newcastle to half chances and the odd set piece threat. They have made things really difficult for the visitors, crowding them out of space on the edge of the area.

When the home side have advanced up the pitch the Newcastle defence has not looked particularly secure.

As we reach the half-hour mark, Newcastle have 10 shots to Millwall’s one, though they sit one apiece on shots on target.

Esse gets caught on his heels as Hall pulls a long ball back on the left, and in the crowd at the top of the box Willock takes a shot, pulling it wide – cheers from the home crowd again.

First piece of good attacking play from Millwall as Neghli and Baggott work on the overlap. Baggott lofts a high ball to the back post, where Dykes gets a foot on it on the volley, but he can’t quite get over it and it’s easily picked up by Hornicek.

Barnes and Ramsey combine again down the left, with the midfielder trying to feed Barnes on his run. The pass has too much on it though, and as it runs out the back it’s met with jeers from the home fans for a goal kick.

Wissa breaks away down the centre of the field, with Barnes on his left, using him as a decoy. Wissa takes the shot though and it is blocked by a sliding defender.

Newcastle hit 20 minutes in with 68 per cent possession but nothing to show yet for their efforts. You feel like it will only be a matter of time though.

Another Newcastle corner, swung in well and Botman comes charging in, beating cooper to a free header. The defender heads it over the bar and holds his head in his hands. The visitors could definitely be a goal up by now.

Hall’s free-kick is met by the first man Metcalfe who heads it away to atone for his foul and Newcastle remain stymied.

Millwall will have expected Newcastle to dominate the ball but they are really pushing for an opener, especially down the left side with Barnes and Hall.

Again, Newcastle coming down the wings, this time on the left. Esse picks the ball up but loses it and Willock picks it up and takes a shot on his right foot with good power but sends it straight at Marschall. The debut keeper parries it away and it’s cleared by a  Millwall header.

Willock comes down the left soon after and is fouled by Metcalfe to get a free kick in a good spot outside the box.

Murphy gets a shot off after Dedic picks up a long ball on the right side and crosses it back towards the middle of the field. Murphy gets on it and takes the shot inside the box off his left foot but it sails over the bar.

González gives the ball away cheaply and Metcalfe picks it up, but unable to move it forward.

Newcastle will need to make sure they don’t get complacent in defence.

Millwall having a spell of possession, the counter-attack looking like their best option but as they move down the right hand side, Lovelace makes a late challenge to get the ball back and fouls Wissa.

Newcastle advancing, with Dedic and Ramsey moving the ball across midfield. Barnes gets the ball on the left of the box, and his ball is in knocked out and Newcastle get the first corner of the game.

Nothing comes of it as it is sent in high and long over the box.

Fair to say both teams are settling, but Millwall try and create a chance with Lovelace, though it’s intercepted. Dykes takes a bit of a knock and is slow to get up.

Here we go in south London, and Millwall get us started.

Just a reminder of the teams starting today:

Starting XI: Filip Marschall; Jordi Osei-Tutu, Caleb Taylor, Jake Cooper, Elkan Baggott; Lyndon Dykes, Jenson Metcalfe; Camiel Neghli, Daniel Kelly, Romain Esse; Zak Lovelace

Substitutes: Regan Monty, Tristan Parkes, Sacha Vieira, George Beaumont, Yanis Issoufou, George Evans, Taïryk Arconte, Alfie Massey, Zak Sturge

Starting XI: Lukás Hornícek; Lewis Hall, Fabian Schär, Amar Dedic, Sven Botman; Jacob Murphy, Nico González; Jacob Ramsey, Harvey Barnes, Joe Willock; Yoane Wissa

Substitutes: Tino Livramento, Anthony Elanga, Malick Thiaw, Nick Pope, Lewis Miley, Bazoumana Touré, Matias Fernandez-Pardo, Aladji Bamba, Sean Steur

The teams are coming out of the tunnel, and both home and away fans in the Den are already in loud voice. Kick off on the way!

"We've tried to find the right balance" ⚖️Matthias Jaissle on his team selection for tonight's match with Millwall ⚫️ pic.twitter.com/kiRRxAgLk8

We’re just a few minutes away from kick off in south London, but Bournemouth have scored the first goal of the third round, with Ryan Christie putting his side ahead against Lincoln.

Alex Neil has not minced his words over his squad’s injury crisis. His team is down 13 players, which the coach says has “definitely forced” his hand in terms of squad rotation.

Playing two matches a week in the “relentless” Championship has turned his squad selection into a “needs must scenario” and he even admitted he “may need to make a couple of changes at half-time depending on how the game goes”

Matthias Jaissle is clearly taking this competition seriously and having started the league well, he is still trying to get the fans onside and create momentum for his team.

At the same time, Telegraph Sport have reported that Ross Wilson, the sporting director, has warned there will have to be more departures in future windows. Having lost Alexander Isak, Anthony Gordon, Sandro Tonali and Bruno Guimarães in 12 months, there will be yet be more upheaval.

You can read Luke Edwards’ full story on that here

The Premier League teams playing in European competitions enter the EFL Cup in this round, with all 16 fixtures being played over five match days. As well as tonight’s games there will be:

Fleetwood Town vs Sheffield United (7.45pm)

*all kick-off at 8pm, unless stated otherwise

Newcastle have named a strong side – probably the strongest they could field when factoring in senior players needing game time – to take on Millwall in the Carabao Cup.

Jacob Ramsey impressed coming off the bench against Bournemouth last weekend and manager Matthias Jaissle refused to sanction winger Jacob Murphy’s transfer to Nottingham Forest late in the window. Both deserve a chance to impress from the start.

Veteran centre back Fabian Schar comes in for Malick Thiaw, but those are the only three changes from the side that drew with Bournemouth.

Jaissle insisted he would take the competition seriously and the teamsheet proves it, but it also raises questions about some of Newcastle’s summer recruitment.

Bazoumana Toure cost £42m but was withdrawn at half time in the win over West Brom in the previous round, which means Harvey Barnes does not get a rest. That’s a lot of money to spend on a winger who has not looked Premier League ready so far.

Aladji Bamba, a £30m signing from Monaco, has not started a game yet and has been an unused substitute since the opening game against Liverpool. He remains on the bench.

Even Sean Steur, who has looked good since his summer move from Ajax, cannot dislodge another more recent arrival in former Manchester City midfielder Nico González.

Having made a total of eight new signings in a much-vaunted summer rebuild, Jaissle only started three of them against Bournemouth and only two start tonight at The Den.

Early days but this was one of the main reasons Eddie Howe quit – he did not think the likes of Toure, Steur and Bamba were ready to play first team football.

The visitors have arrived in south London

We've made it to South East London 👋 pic.twitter.com/nh8Fpa37xT

Your Mags at Millwall ✊ pic.twitter.com/zfnHgTlWgh

Keeper Filip Marschall is making his debut while Jensen Metcalfe is back in the squad after his red card against Bolton was overturned on appeal

How your Lions line-up tonight 🔢 pic.twitter.com/wEp6qLIz4Y

Welcome to tonight’s live coverage of Millwall vs Newcastle United, as the Geordies travel to south London for the third round of the Carabao Cup.

Newcastle held off West Brom in their second-round match, with Harvey Barnes scoring two second-half goals to see his side through. It was a mighty comeback, after Isaac Price scored early to stun the crowd at St James’ Park. Bazoumana Toure equalised for Matthias Jaissle’s side just before half-time, and Barnes, his replacement in the second half, put them ahead minutes after the restart. West Brom pulled it back to 2-2 with a penalty converted by Price after Lewis Hall was deemed to have handled the ball in the box, but Barnes got his second just nine minutes from full-time and the hosts were able to see out the match to progress.

Alex Neil’s Millwall have reached round three via a 0-1 win over Cambridge United, following a penalty shoot-out in the first round to beat QPR. They come into this tie with a squad stretched thin, as they have been hit with an injury crisis a month into the new season. Millwall have confirmed that they will be without Casper De Norre, Josh Coburn, Tristan Crama, Alfie Doughty, Mathis Servais, Ryan Leonard, Mihailo Ivanovic, Lukas Jensen and Luke Cundle.

Both sides sit seventh in their respective leagues, with Millwall on a record of three wins and two losses this season, while Newcastle remain unbeaten (two draws and a win).

Newcastle will hoping to progress smoothly in a tournament that they have recently enjoyed good form in – winners in 2025 and semi-finalists last season – and with Millwall dealing with a bare bones squad, the Championship side are the underdogs on paper going into this fixture.

But, as always, anything can happen, so let us know your score prediction in the comments and we’ll be bringing you team news soon!

#1472. England star Ollie Watkins' wife Ellie flees their new life in Saudi Arabia amid deadly missile attacks - just months after £50m move to the Middle East

Published: 09:41 EDT, 3 November 2026 | Updated: 12:23 EDT, 3 November 2026

England striker Ollie Watkins' wife Ellie is fleeing Saudi Arabia to seek 'normality' for their children amid deadly missile attacks in the Middle East.

Ollie and Ellie, 31 and 30, moved to Saudi capital Riyadh in the summer with their two children after a £51million transfer from Aston Villa to Al-Hilal. But the recent deadly re-escalation of the Houthi-Saudi Arabia conflict has sparked a move back home for the family - with no end date in sight.

The Watkins family have two young children - Amara, five, and three-year-old Marley. Ellie initially admitted she had broken down in tears over the move but later felt 'everything was coming together'. Ellie and the children are now fleeing.

'We've had a bit of a plot twist,' Ellie said in a post on TikTok today. 'I have come back to the UK for, hopefully, a little bit. I don't actually know when.

Major airports in Saudi Arabia are operating reduced services after a missile attack by Yemen's Houthi movement on Riyadh's airport killed 13 people. Two people were also killed after an attack at King Fahd International Airport in Dammam.

'There's just a little bit of conflict and things going on over in Saudi and we basically decided just to stay here until it calms down,' Ellie added.

Ollie Watkins and wife Ellie moved to Saudi Arabia following his £50m summer transfer (Source: Instagram/Ellie Watkins)

Ellie has now returned to the UK amid missile attacks in Saudi (Source: Instagram/Ellie Watkins)

'I felt like I needed to do that for the kids so there is some form of normality until we can get back out there and all be together.'

Husband Ollie is hoping for a call-up to the England squad this week and will continue to play in the Saudi Pro League while his family reside in the UK.

Saudi football experts have suggested the striker, who has five goals and five assists in eight Saudi Pro League appearances so far, earns 'a minimum of £20million a year' - tax-free.

Al-Hilal play Shabab AlAhli, of Dubai, in the Asian Champions League today.

Ollie and Ellie have been settling into a new home, redecorating and finding schools for their children in Riyadh. Those plans have now been derailed.

Meanwhile, football's 2027 Asia Cup has been delayed by almost a year amid the ongoing Middle East crisis. The Six Kings Slam tennis exhibition event has also been called off while Formula One is expected to move its end-of-season races.

Ellie had said moving to Saudi Arabia has 'been a lot' but 'everything's finally coming together' - posting photos of their new life together (Source: Instagram/Ellie Watkins)

The WAG shared a snap of their stylish living room as she added: 'Everything's finally coming together and we're so happy in our new home' (Source: Instagram/Ellie Watkins)

Less than two months before it was due to kick off, the Asia Cup was today postponed until December 2027.

It makes the tournament not only a logistical nightmare for the 24 participating teams but also raises serious safety concerns.

A statement from the Asian Football Confederation said: 'The Organising Committee for AFC Asian Cup approved rescheduling the flagship national team tournament considering the current exceptional circumstances arising from developments in the region, including substantial logistical complexities and travel disruptions.

'The new dates of the tournament (December 23 2027 to January 21 2028) will be presented to FIFA for approval.

'Exceptional circumstances have been created for the organisation and delivery of the Competition as originally scheduled, making the postponement necessary in the interest of all participating teams, officials, spectators and other stakeholders.'

However, the delay boosts several Premier League clubs, who no longer face losing players for up to a month of the season. Japan had ten Premier League players available for selection, with Aston Villa potentially losing first-choice goalkeeper Zion Suzuki.

#1471. My Everton #178: What Makes It The People's Club

It all started with my dad who used to go to both Everton and Liverpool games well before my time.

Over the years, he started a family and, thankfully, his allegiances started to move towards Everton.

Jimmy, my eldest brother, came along years later and he started following the Blues straight away, going to the games as soon as he was allowed to.

I came along in 1984 and soon became the newest Blue in the house.

From the age of around 10, Jimmy took me to my first game at Goodison and I fell in love with Everton from that day. Me and Jimmy went to every home game and a few of the local away fixtures as well.

Our dad didn’t really go to many games with us. He did start coming again around 1999 but had a heart attack after one of the games. He never went again – but followed from the couch at home.

Moving forward some years Jimmy met his future wife, Christine, who at the time was a Leeds fan... not for long, though! It took only three games watching the Blues to convert her and extend our home seats by another.

We loved the tradition of a home game day: the meet-up at my mum and dad's house and the drive listening to Radio City’s football talk.

We had season tickets for many years until Christine became ill and needed constant treatment. We all decided to give them up and buy each game separately if and when we could around her treatment.

Unfortunately, after a year, Christine lost her battle and left us. Jimmy needed to get back to Goodison as soon as possible, so again, we all started going to every game together.

Skip through to 2024 and our dad passed away. Another blue light gone out.

Me and Jimmy made sure to remember him at the new stadium with a stone and photo inside.

Jimmy was obsessed with the new stadium build, watching drone progress daily. He waited so long for a new stadium. Unfortunately, Jimmy also passed away just two months after our dad, not getting to step inside the new stadium he always dreamed of.

Again, with losing my dad and Jimmy, who I always went the game with, I decided that I would also stop going.

For the past two seasons I've supported from home, but all while still singing the Blues!

Family is what makes Everton the People's Club.

Its love is passed down through each family member. All those years ago my dad could have chosen the red side but didn’t.

Since then, at least 15 family members have supported and followed the Blues.

I still haven't been a game at our new stadium, but Jimmy and Christine's grandkids do, singing in his name.

My Everton shares first-hand accounts describing the most-treasured memories of fans, players, and staff both past and present.

#1470. From Jose Mourinho's Sevilla disaster to Erik ten Hag's dismal group stage exit: Man United's litany of Champions League humiliations since Sir Alex Ferguson - as Michael Carrick fights for his job ahead of Roma clash

Published: 18:02 EDT, 2 November 2026 | Updated: 12:27 EDT, 3 November 2026

Michael Carrick and Manchester United are enduring the club's worst start to a league season in 40 years, with the Red Devils languishing in 17th place.

Their woes in recent years have been well documented, with the club seemingly incapable of finding anyone to match the glory days under Sir Alex Ferguson.

Since his departure in 2013, they have had eight managers – seven of whom have managed them in Europe's biggest competition.

The three-time champions of Europe have performed particularly poorly in the Champions League in that time, not making it past the quarter-finals once in seven attempts.

They have won less than half of their Champions League fixtures since Ferguson left – and only 34 per cent in the current decade.

Carrick brought United back into the Champions League last season but since being given the permanent role has hit shocking form

And they will be lucky to even reach that stage this season if they continue to play as they have been in the competition, losing to Atletico Madrid away and being embarrassed by Champions League debutants Como.

With United set to take on Roma on Tuesday in their fourth game of the competition, Daily Mail Sport takes a look at how each manager on United's carousel has fared in the Champions League... and where it unravelled for all of them.

It feels as if it has been an age since David Moyes took the reins at Old Trafford. The Scotsman had a torrid time in his ten-month spell at United.

His tenure was characterised by embarrassing losses, a lack of consistency and an inability to transition from the old regime.

Moyes was sacked in April after a 2-0 loss to his old Everton side that ended United's hopes of a top-four finish for that season. He was already under serious pressure having been dumped out of the Champions League in the quarter-finals by Bayern Munich.

Moyes was handpicked by Ferguson to replace him but didn't even last a season at United

The current Everton manager oversaw a 1-1 draw at home in the first leg, with Nemanja Vidic's goal being cancelled out by Bastian Schweinsteiger – who moved to Old Trafford a year later. But Bayern – managed by Pep Guardiola – quickly responded to Patrice Evra's goal in the second leg to win it 3-1.

They had to battle to even get that far, with a comfortable group stage – four wins and two draws – being followed by an embarrassing 2-0 defeat at Olympiacos in the first leg of the last 16. A Robin van Persie hat-trick in the second leg spared their blushes.

The big Dutchman came to United with a stellar CV having won both the Champions League and UEFA Cup with Ajax in the 90s, as well as league titles in Spain and Germany.

And he seemed the exact kind of serial winner who would be the perfect replacement for Ferguson, but it just didn't work out. Van Gaal spent heavily in the market when he arrived - most notably breaking the British transfer record to secure the services of Angel Di Maria for £59.7million - but he simply couldn't find his feet in England.

Van Gaal had just the one season in the Champions League with United before leaving, and it was possibly the most disastrous since Ferguson's departure.

They were placed in a group with Wolfsburg, PSV and CSKA Moscow, and were dumped out at the earliest possible stage, finishing third in the group with just eight points. They fell into the Europa League and - after overturning a disastrous 2-1 defeat by Danish side Midtjylland in the first leg of their last-32 game - were sent packing by Liverpool.

Joining in 2016 after being sacked by Chelsea, Jose Mourinho immediately got busy in the market.

And initially it seemed as if he was going to make it work. Paul Pogba and Zlatan Ibrahimovic arrived and United won their first three games. Although their league form dipped, they did go on to win the League Cup and the Europa League in that first season.

But then it all began to fall away. Like Van Gaal and Moyes before him, Mourinho only got one try at his favourite competition with United, and exited in a less than graceful manner.

Jose won the Europa League whilst in Manchester but never really found success in the big competition

He may have won it with Porto in 2004 and Inter six years later but at United he only got as far as the round of 16, and crashed out after a 2-1 home defeat by Sevilla following a 0-0 draw in the first leg.

Recently Jose revealed that his relationship with the Red Devils was very nearly different. In his new Netflix biopic, Mourinho, he said that he had agreed to take over straight after Ferguson - only to be lured back to Chelsea by Roman Abramovich instead. Who knows how he would have fared at Old Trafford if he had joined three years earlier.

Mourinho's successor also had an excellent start to life in the United dugout but ended up being hounded out after a tumultuous three years.

When Ole was at the wheel, at first it seemed like United were on course to return to the big time however, slowly but surely, it became clear that it wasn't going to work out.

Solskjaer is one of two men on this list to have won the Champions League with United as a player and the Norwegian scored arguably the most historic goal in United's European history, getting the dramatic winner in the 1999 final.

And he is probably the only gaffer since Ferguson to have had a positive memorable moment in the competition. It came in Paris in March of 2019, shortly after he took over. After losing 2-0 at home in the first leg of the tie they looked like they were already out but miraculously Ole masterminded a 3-1 victory and won on away goals.

Unfortunately that is where the good times as a manager in the Champions League end. After the PSG win United were beaten 4-0 on aggregate by Barcelona and then didn't make it into the competition for the 2019-20 season.

They did return with Ole in 2020-21 - only to be knocked out in the group stage, finishing third in a group with PSG, RB Leipzig and Turkish side Basaksehir. They went on to reach the Europa League final that year - losing to Villarreal on penalties - and Solskjaer was gone in November, before the end of next season's group stage.

Taking over as interim manager until the end of the 2021-22 campaign - following a caretaker spell from a certain Michael Carrick - Austrian Rangnick was in charge for just three European games.

The final game of the group stage saw a 1-1 draw with Swiss side Young Boys, with Mason Greenwood scoring United's goal.

Then they took on Atletico Madrid in the last-16, and after a 1-1 draw away, were sent packing with a 1-0 second-leg defeat at Old Trafford.

Renan Lodi's header for Atletico Madrid sent United crashing out under Ralf Rangnick

Rangnick's spell at United is best remembered for his forthright assessments of the club's dire situation, and he famously likened their situation to that of a patient needing open-heart surgery.

'You don’t even need glasses to see and analyse where the problems are,' he said. 'Now it’s about how do we solve them? It’s not enough to do some minor amendments. In medicine you would say that this is an operation of the open heart.

'If this happens and everyone has realised that this has to happen and if people want to work together then it makes sense and I believe it doesn’t take two or three years to change those things. This can happen within one year.'

More than four years on, the fans are still waiting.

Erik ten Hag came in nine years after Ferguson's exit, and while he brought a League Cup and an FA Cup to Old Trafford it was not enough to stop him being sacked.

Like Van Gaal and Solskjaer, Ten Hag's United failed to make it past the group stage of the Champions League. He actually fared even worse than his predecessors by finishing rock bottom of the group in the 2023-24 season, after particularly rough losses away to Copenhagen and Galatasaray.

Like Van Gaal and Solskjaer, Ten Hag's United failed to make it past the group stage of the Champions League

After a dismal eighth-placed finish in the Premier League the FA Cup win over Manchester City ended that season on a high - and saved Ten Hag's job.

He even signed a contract extension that summer, but was ditched by October with United 14th.

Ruben Amorim, who replaced Ten Hag, did not manage United in the Champions League - though he did reach the Europa League final with them in 2025.

His sacking in January this year paved the way for Michael Carrick to join as interim and, in steering them to third place, ensured United were back at Europe's top table after two seasons away.

That also won him the permanent role, but Carrick has had a torrid start to the new campaign - winning just two of his side's 13 games in all competitions and setting a new club record for the longest winless streak in the Premier League era (nine).

One of those wins was in the Champions League against Azerbaijani minnows Sabah, but they followed that with the defeats by Atletico Madrid and Como.

Carrick will hope United can finally arrest this run of form at home to Roma on Tuesday, but it will not be easy with the Italians enjoying an excellent start to the season and currently sitting third in Serie A.

A win, however, could keep Carrick in a job and breathe some life into a United team that desperately needs it.

#1469. An open structure-guided RNA foundation model for generalizable prediction

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

RNA language models have achieved strong performance across diverse downstream tasks by leveraging large-scale sequence data. However, RNA function is fundamentally shaped by hierarchical structure, making structural information important for pre-training. Existing approaches often depend on noisy annotations or task-specific objectives that can limit generalizability. Here we present structRFM, a structure-guided RNA foundation model trained on 21 million RNA sequence–structure pairs by integrating base-pairing interactions into masked language modelling through a pair-matching operation. We also introduce MUSES, a multi-source ensemble of secondary structures designed to mitigate predictor bias, and a dynamic masking ratio that balances structure-guided and nucleotide-level masking. structRFM learns joint sequence and structure representations as sequence-level, nucleotide-level and pairwise features for broad downstream adaptation. It ranks highly in zero-shot homology classification and establishes new benchmarks for secondary-structure prediction. Its tertiary-structure adaptation, Zfold, consistently improves both three-dimensional predictions and their extracted secondary structures, with performance comparable to AlphaFold31 across CASP15-natural, CASP16 and RNA-Puzzles. structRFM also improves performance on function-prediction tasks and generalizes to newly released RNA families and long non-coding RNAs. Together, these results demonstrate the effectiveness of structure-guided pre-training and highlight multimodal RNA language models for robust structural and functional inference. The complete 21-million-pair dataset, model weights and source code are openly available to support multimodal RNA foundation-model development.

a Ternary simplex visualization of the MUSES performance landscape across weighted combination configurations. Each vertex corresponds to a single standalone method (BPfold, ViennaRNA or CONTRAfold), and interior points represent weighted ensemble models. We normalized weighting coefficients for proportional equivalence and applied linear interpolation over a dense grid to smooth the INF metric distribution. Colour gradients (blue to red) represent INF values, with contour lines for enhanced resolution. This visualization illustrates how ensemble weighting modulates MUSES performance for robust secondary-structure annotation and identifies optimal weight-coefficient regimes with associated trade-offs. b Benchmark evaluation of six established multi-source RNA secondary-structure prediction methods23,24,25,26,34,44,45,79 on the Rfam66,67 and full ArchiveII37 (n = 3, 975 independent RNA sequences) datasets, stratified by three sequence-length categories (≤ 500 nt, 501–1000 nt, > 1000 nt). c Linear fits extrapolating prediction performance for the six methods on both datasets. Lines are linear regression fits, and shaded bands represent 95% confidence intervals. A substantial performance degradation is observed with increasing sequence length, highlighting the current challenge of modelling RNA secondary structures for long RNA sequences.

a Head-to-head comparison of structRFM with other models using ϵRMSD72, TM-score73, GDT-TS74 and INF75. Circle size indicates the absolute difference between the two methods. b Violin plots of RMSD values. For each method in b, n = 8 independent RNA targets for CASP15-natural, n = 13 independent RNA targets for CASP16, and n = 20 independent RNA targets for RNA-Puzzles. The inner box plots show the median (white centre line), 25th and 75th percentiles (lower and upper bounds of the thick line), and minimum and maximum (lower and upper thin whiskers).

The ϵRMSD, TM-score and GDT-TS of tertiary structures, together with the INF of secondary structures extracted from tertiary structures, are annotated. In the secondary-structure diagrams, stems are shown in green, multiple loops in red, interior loops in yellow, hairpin loops in blue, and 5′ and 3′ unpaired regions in orange. In general, structRFM performs better on natural targets than on synthetic targets containing dense long-range interactions, but sometimes fails to predict short local stems (in green), resulting in large multiple loops (in red).

The ϵRMSD, TM-score and GDT-TS of tertiary structures, together with the INF of secondary structures extracted from tertiary structures, are annotated. In the secondary-structure diagrams, stems are shown in green, multiple loops in red, interior loops in yellow, hairpin loops in blue, and 5’ and 3’ unpaired regions in orange. In general, structRFM performs better on viral and aptamer targets but performs worse on multimer and bacterial targets. For targets marked with blue circles, the sequences used for CASP16 prediction differ substantially from those of the PDB ground-truth structures because regions unresolved in the experimental structures were not modelled.

a Overall comparison of methods for IRES identification using seven metrics. b Overall comparison of methods for ncRNA classification using seven metrics. c PR and ROC curves for the 13 individual classes in the nRC dataset.

a Distribution of sequence lengths, with most RNA sequences centred around 250 nucleotides. b Number and distribution of RNA families (categories). rRNA and tRNA dominate the dataset, accounting for 66.3% and 16.7%, respectively. c Composition of base-pairing interactions in secondary structures. Canonical base pairs represent approximately half of all interactions, including GC (26.5%), AU (14.4%) and GU (7.2%) pairs. d Distribution of confidence scores for predicted secondary structures. #1468. Everton's Remembrance Day Plans

Everton and Coventry City will come together ahead of Friday’s Premier League fixture at Hill Dickinson Stadium to remember the fallen and honour the sacrifices made by servicemen and women during conflict.

The pre-match Remembrance ceremony will involve players and staff from both clubs, as well as representatives of the Royal Navy, British Army, Royal Air Force and Merchant Navy.

Those taking part in the tribute will include serving personnel from the Tri-Service Toffees Supporters’ Club and former servicemen and women supported by Everton in the Community’s Veterans Programme.

Supporters are requested to arrive to their seats from 7.50pm, ahead of the ceremony, which will follow the walk-out by the teams and match officials.

As part of the Remembrance ceremony, the captains of Everton and Coventry City will lay commemorative poppy wreaths on the pitch ahead of kick-off, along with representatives from the Armed Forces, the Tri-Service Toffees and Everton in the Community.

Players from both sides will wear shirts bearing the poppy emblem, in memory of the fallen.

We will proudly welcome the following service personnel to take part in our pre-match tribute:

The following former service personnel will also participate in the tribute through Everton in the Community’s Veterans Programme:

Following the laying of the wreaths, The Last Post will be performed by bugler Andrew Manning.

As a mark of respect, the traditional pre-match siren will not sound before the teams enter the pitch, though Z-Cars will play as normal.

As part of the Club’s recognition of serving personnel, Steve McCann and Danny Jackson, both members of Tri-Service Toffees, will take part in the half-time Hit the Bar competition.

The Tri-Service Toffees is an affiliated Everton supporters’ club for those serving in the Royal Navy, British Army and Royal Air Force, whether regular or reservist. Evertonians interested in joining or finding out more about the supporters’ club should email triservicetoffees@gmail.com.

Shirts worn by Everton’s Men’s and Women’s players during the Remembrance period will be auctioned to raise vital funds to support the work of the Royal British Legion. To find out more – or to bid for a shirt – click here.

What Remembrance Means to Me – A Message From The Tri-Service Toffees

Remembrance is about remembering. It really is that simple.

Remembering the sacrifices made by so many, from the First World War through every conflict since. Not just those who served in uniform, but the families, friends, colleagues and civilians whose lives were forever changed.

It is about taking a moment to acknowledge those sacrifices, both great and small, and the individuals who made them.

Having served for over 37 years, including numerous operational tours in conflict, I don’t reflect on my own sacrifices. Those will be for others to remember when I am gone.

Instead, I remember my mum, who served in the Royal Navy, and my uncles Tony and Frank (her brothers). All three have now passed away, but each played a significant part in inspiring my own military career. I also remember the friends and colleagues who have made the ultimate sacrifice in the hope of making a difference.

But perhaps the person foremost in my thoughts is my wife, Shirley.

Throughout my military career, she has made countless sacrifices of her own, often quietly and without recognition. Like so many military spouses and families, she has carried burdens that others rarely see, whilst asking for little in return.

Their sacrifices deserve our remembrance, too.

So, when you pause to remember, think not only of those who gave their lives in service to our nation, but also of those closest to you, whose sacrifices may never have been publicly acknowledged.

At the going down of the sun and in the morning, we will remember them.

Major Anthony John Sandle RLC, Second-in-Command, 156 Regiment, The Royal Logistic Corps(pictured above with Everton Ambassador Graham Stuart)

#1467. Martin O'Neill's greatest mistake was staying after winning the league

By CALUM CROWE, SCOTTISH DEPUTY CHIEF SPORTS WRITER

Published: 12:24 EDT, 3 November 2026 | Updated: 14:51 EDT, 3 November 2026

Winning the league title in such dramatic fashion on the final day of last season, Martin O’Neill should have recognised the moment for what it was. The End.

In a chaotic season where he had rescued Celtic from oblivion not once but twice, that was the moment when the credits should have rolled.

The blockbuster Hollywood finale. The perfect opportunity to go out in a blaze of glory and sail off into the sunset, his legacy not only secure but further enhanced.

His decision to stay on as manager this season has proven to be a mistake. In his heart of hearts, O’Neill must realise this. The whole thing is done. Finished. Finito. Terminado, as one of his predecessors would have said.

On the back of the 2-0 defeat to Falkirk last weekend, it has now reached the point where O’Neill’s continued presence at the club is damaging his legacy.

The fans are turning on him. They don’t care what he did for the club 20-odd years ago. They aren’t interested in his wisecracks. They don’t want to hear nostalgic tales of old about how things used to be.

They care only about the here and now and about what they are watching on the pitch. Now mired in a run of three wins in their last ten matches, O’Neill’s side are, if anything, actually getting worse.

O’Neill’s argument about still being top of the league is one of deflection, denial and delusion. Complete and utter claptrap. It is an insult to the intelligence of Celtic supporters.

Martin O'Neill's Celtic team lead the table but have struggled to convince

This is the problem. If there is solid evidence to support the claims that he has lost the faith of the players, then he is also rapidly losing the faith of the fans.

In a way, it is sad that it should come to this. The man is 74 years old. He didn’t ask to be thrust back into the spotlight. At least, not initially.

On two occasions, he answered an SOS call from Dermot Desmond last season. He came back and he did exactly what was asked of him.

If Celtic had any sort of competent succession plan in place, there wouldn’t even have been a conversation around O’Neill’s future towards the end of last season.

It would have been a case of shaking his hand, thanking him enormously for a heroic contribution, before being serenaded by supporters one last time after winning a league and cup double.

Yet, going back to those final few weeks of last season, it was clear O’Neill had the bug for it once again. He was never going to walk away, and nor were the board ever going to turn him down.

In the end, the situation needed one of two things to happen. It either needed O’Neill to save himself from his own desires, and have some sense and foresight about how the club was being run, or it needed Celtic to show some vision and make a proper long-term appointment.

In the absence of both, it was the blind leading the blind. O’Neill hung around primarily to have another crack at Europe, the Celtic board thought they had a bulletproof shield by retaining the services of a club icon.

The argument that kept on being trotted out at the time centred on how winning the league title meant that O’Neill had earned the right to stay on.

But that fundamentally missed the point. Of course he had earned the right. He’s Martin O’Neill. Only Jock Stein stands above him in the pantheon of the club’s all-time greatest managers.

Fans adored him (yes, past tense). But just because he had earned the right doesn’t mean it was the right thing to do. That’s the key difference.

Celtic manager Martin O'Neill lifts the league trophy back in May

Whenever Manchester United inevitably sack Michael Carrick, let’s suppose for a second that Sir Alex Ferguson comes in and takes charge for a few games.

Everything goes well, the team start winning games again, everyone starts getting those old feelings coming back.

But would it mean that the right thing to do is to hand Sir Alex the job for another season? Of course it wouldn’t.

The failure to separate that nostalgia and love for O’Neill from what was required moving into this season was a catastrophic error of judgment on Celtic’s part.

The club had absolutely no idea how to move forward in the summer – just like they would have absolutely no idea who to appoint now if O’Neill was to be relieved of his duties.

In the past, Celtic sacked Tommy Burns. They sacked Billy McNeill. The belief that O’Neill could not suffer a similar fate is hugely naive.

Right now, a growing section of the fanbase view him as little more than an extension of Desmond. His status as a club icon is fading.

Over the weekend, a couple of articles surfaced from a few years ago when O’Neill was sacked as Nottingham Forest manager in 2019.

They spoke of how O’Neill eventually lost the dressing room and of how the players were left bemused by his lack of detail on the tactical side of the game.

Some Celtic fans view O'Neill as little more than an extension of major shareholder Dermot Desmond

The parallels with this current Celtic side are obvious. Just look at the comments from Callum McGregor and Cameron Carter-Vickers over recent weeks.

They are a team with absolutely no tactical identity – and it’s difficult to see how this gets any better for as long as O’Neill, along with coaches Shaun Maloney and Mark Fotheringham, remain at the helm.

O’Neill attended a Q&A session at a supporter’s club in Greenock on Monday night, along with chief executive Michael Nicholson and chairman Brian Wilson.

A bizarre announcement from Celtic yesterday claimed that the questioning had been ‘hard but fair’ as supporters voiced their concerns about the current malaise.

The one man who continues to dodge the Paxman treatment is, of course, Desmond himself, the club’s largest shareholder who operates as the commander-in-chief.

And the one question which is now becoming painfully unavoidable is this: what grounds are there for Martin O’Neill to continue as Celtic manager?

#1466. Man City survive tunnel clash and Porto fury thanks to Haaland double

Erling Haaland revealed on the eve of this clash how he loves chopping firewood in his spare time – and his goals set alight Manchester City’s Champions League campaign on a fractious evening in Porto.

So much for the new group stage of the competition taking time to warm up. This clash was a hot-blooded, bitter contest that spilt over in the tunnel at half-time, with players getting separated and tempers rising.

And City were not easing themselves back into European action either, they went full throttle at the start of a tough set of group games. With Enzo Maresca, it looks like it will be all-out attack to get the best out of this team.

They can look nervous at the back, particularly with the ball at Gianluigi Donnarumma’s feet, but have attacking weapons to hurt any team in this elite competition. This was a performance that their rivals will take note of.

“It was a complete performance on and off the ball for 95 minutes,” was Maresca’s assessment.

City will certainly scare the traditional heavyweights with Haaland leading their attack and taking an axe to Porto’s defence like he does with logs in his back garden. It was his 58th and 59th goal in 59 games in the Champions League, with his latest an expertly directed header off a post and a calm side-footed finish.

NO MISTAKE from Erling Haaland this time 💪He's put Man City 1-0 up in Porto 🇵🇹 pic.twitter.com/UpKOqQA49s

There is an argument that Pep Guardiola could have achieved more in the Champions League, given City’s dominance in domestic football. They have been knocked out by Real Madrid in the last three seasons but this is a new City, different personnel and even a new look.

They wore their black and yellow away kit, inspired by “Manchester’s iconic worker bee” according to Puma, and grafted their way to victory here. Non-stop running going forward, and scrapping with Porto, too.

The Portuguese champions were not happy with Marc Guéhi’s challenge on Gabri Veiga and claimed an elbow was used, with the row carrying on in the tunnel at half-time with security guards separating the players. Rúben Dias also appeared to nudge a Porto official on his way to the dressing room.

“I didn’t see anything but anyway, you can ask how many times you see me or my bench stand up? Zero, for 95 minutes. How many times do you see their bench? So...” Maresca added.

Only Dias and Haaland remain from the starting line-up from the Champions League triumph three years ago, so this is essentially a new team with a new manager.

Erling Haaland seals the deal in Porto 🤝🇵🇹 pic.twitter.com/10xSTtZ8nw

Phil Foden, on as a sub in that game, started at Estádio do Dragão after his horse Wreck It Ronnie defeated Najidi Storm, which started the Goodwood race with 1-33 odds and is now the shortest-priced loser in British racing history. The rest of the team are new to City’s challenge.

That includes Ayyoub Bouaddi, 18, who was part of a £320m midfield refresh following the departure of Rodri, who was named among the Ballon d’Or nominees a few hours before kick-off to highlight the experience and class City have lost.

Bouaddi, who cost £81.4m from Lille, made a good start in his full debut. The Moroccan teenager is neat on the ball and gets around the pitch, with the next step being able to dominate games like his predecessor.

“In his last game he lost two balls and stayed calm and was back in our box,” Maresca said. “This shows how good he is because any player after two [poor] passes panics, but he is just 18. Erling, Rúben, Mateo [Kovacic], they can manage these kind of games better, but you don’t expect it from a guy of 18. I didn’t see him panic.”

By Bouaddi’s side in midfield was Enzo Fernández, who sought to drive forward into space when City counter-attacked. He was among the players who, along with Dias, were reminded of their Benfica history by the home fans.

Diogo Costa tends to be linked with a move to the Premier League every summer, but has been a one-club man for his career so far. But he showed why clubs are looking at him with his first-half saves to deny Haaland and Rayan Cherki.

Porto’s legendary goalkeeper, Helton, was in the press box at half-time and would have been impressed with the saves, although he was not in his seat when Haaland scored the first goal, which came 94 seconds after the restart.

City had worked the ball around the penalty area, with Antoine Semenyo drawing out Costa before laying off to Fernández. Haaland’s header from the cross had such precision that the goalkeeper did not dive as it angled in off a post.

Still, Porto had their chances with Alberto Costa heading wide from a corner and William Gomes charging down a Donnarumma kick – with City’s most nervous moments coming when they passed around their back line.

Man City are living dangerously here! 🫣Donnarumma nearly gifts Porto an equaliser 😬 pic.twitter.com/otIfZTHmdn

But Haaland sealed the win as the game ticked into stoppage time, finding the bottom corner from Rayan Aït-Nouri’s cutback.

“It was an amazing game against the champions of Portugal. We knew it would be a difficult fight, man against man, they are a top team,” Haaland said. “They play amazing football. All the pressure, we have to deliver on the big stage and that’s what we did. We controlled the whole first half, created chances.”

For Maresca, the victory was also a challenge against Porto’s aggression, with the Italian coach adding: “I was very pleased. We know in this kind of game when you come here it’s always difficult or tricky. The environment, the way they grew up, it’s normal, but I think we dealt with that very good.”

Top performance, Enzo 👊✨ pic.twitter.com/ds0f207tpS

If you think you can come to a place like this and play and not concede any chances, that is not realistic and it is normal. I am quite lucky as I have a squad of good players. The final whistle is blown and Manchester City begin their Champions League campaign with a 2-0 win in Porto. Erling Haaland’s double gives Enzo Maresca a victory in his first Champions League game in charge of Manchester City.

Enzo has two shots from range in quick succession, one from a free-kick. The free-kick goes just wide and the second is saved by D Costa.

It has been an ill-tempered game and tempers have boiled over again. Rosario and Haaland are involved in a tussle on the floor, which then leads to a mass melee. Haaland and Rosario are both booked for their part in starting that. Haaland is pleased that he got booked but I am not sure why. Both played their part in that melee.

Enzo Maresca’s side will head home with all three points. Ait-Nouri’s cross from the left side of the box picks out Haaland, who first-time shot from 10 yards out picks out the far corner. A clinical finish from Haaland and Manchester City will start their Champions League campaign with a win.

Erling Haaland seals the deal in Porto 🤝🇵🇹 pic.twitter.com/10xSTtZ8nw

That is really poor refereeing. Porto are denied two clear fouls before Rosario is then punished for a foul on Enzo, which was a foul but so too were the previous two incidents. Francesco Farioli is then booked for his protestations but you can understand their frustration.

Ait-Nouri has the chance to warp up the three points with an effort from the edge of the box but his shot with his weaker right foot goes narrowly wide.

Nothing comes from the corner as Hwang’s delivery to the front post is dreadful.

Haaland has his fourth headed chance of the game but this one goes over the bar from Ndiaye’s cross. Haaland has scored one of those chances but spurned some good ones.

Down the other end, Fofana, only just on, wins Porto a corner and whips up the home fans.

Whilst Manchester City’s lead is only 1-0, Porto will believe an equaliser is there for them. However, the momentum they were building 10/15 minutes ago has seemingly been lost and the visitors have managed to wrestle back a bit more control.

That is a big chance missed by Pepe. Gimenez receives it down the left and pings a cross to the back post. The cross perfectly picks out Pepe, who fluffs his lines and completely mis-kicks.

Manchester City are making their final two substitutions of the night as Kovacic and Ait-Nouri come on for Bouaddi and Foden. Ait-Nouri looks like he is going to play left wing.

Two more changes for Porto as Silva and M Fernandes are replaced by Gimenez and Moura.

Porto are going to make their first two changes of the night as Hwang and former Norwich man Sainz come on. Varela and Gomes head off.

For the second time in the half, Donnarumma is lucky. To be fair to the Manchester City keeper, the pass back to him is poor but he is then fortunate. His attempted ball out to his left is intercepted by Gomes but it rolls behind for a goal kick. That ball could have rolled straight into the Manchester City net or fallen straight back at Gomes feet with an empty net ahead of him. Donnarumma was very lucky on Saturday against Coventry to avoid a calamitous moment and he is lucky to avoid another awful moment for the second time in quick succession.

Enzo Maresca responds to a shift in momentum in this game making a double change. Anderson and Ndiaye come on for Cherki and Semenyo.

Porto have started to gain some momentum and they want a penalty. Bouaddi is perhaps a touch fortunate not to be penalised for a foul right on the edge of the box but it may have been just outside the penalty area. You can feel the game starting to turn in Porto’s favour.

Varela is inches away from an equaliser for Porto and plenty of the home fans thought the ball was in the net. Varela sends a curling effort towards goal from the edge of the box but it goes narrowly wide.

Donnrumma is a very, very lucky man. Porto would have had a certain penalty as Donnarumma completely flattened Pepe but the latter was offside so it is no penalty. Donnarumma has been booked but avoids a penalty, which would have been a guarantee had Pepe been onside.

It has been a positive start for Unai Emery’s Aston Villa out in Belgium as they lead Club Brugge 3-1 at half-time.

Enzo Maresca takes charge of his first Champions League game in charge of Manchester City as they have travelled to Portugal to take on Porto at the Estadio do Dragao. These sides last met during the Champions League group stages during the 2020/21 season. Manchester City won 3-1 at home before the two sides drew 0-0 in this stadium.

Manchester City were busy late on in the transfer window, bringing in both Iliman Ndiaye and Enzo Fernandez as they spent nearly £200m on deadline day alone. They come into tonight’s game off the back of three straight Premier League victories to kick off the Maresca era. Maresca has limited Champions League experience as a manager, which came with Chelsea last season. Manchester City have won their opening game of a Champions League campaign in six of the last seven seasons but this will be the first time since 2015/16 that Manchester City embark on a Champions League campaign without Pep Guardiola at the helm.

“It is a hard place to come [Porto],” said Maresca. “They have started really well. In the last 14/15 games in Europe they lost just one, that shows a difficult place to come, but we will try our best and try to win the game. It is a very, very good team. They have different players, but in terms of the team it is very clear in the way they play. They are aggressive without the ball and on the ball, they have a clear style. But we will try our best and try to win the game. The ambition is the same; try to be ourselves and to win games and then we will see.”

Porto, managed by Francesco Farioli, have won every league game so far this season and already sit four points clear at the summit of Liga Portugal. Farioli takes charge of his first game as a manger in the Champions League and the club make their return to the elite European competition after two seasons away.

“We are going to face one of the big favourites to win the competition,” Farioli said. “It will be a game that will demand that we be at our best, and we know that whenever we step onto the Dragão pitch, something special can happen. I am happy to be in the Champions League for the first time at 37 years old. This will be my first game, but we approach every game with the same attention to detail and the same focus. It is easy for the players to be motivated tomorrow [tonight]. But the key will be our strategy and our ability to execute it, individually and collectively.”

Porto were in the Europa League last season, making it to the quarter-finals, where they were knocked out by Nottingham Forest 2-1 on aggregate. The omens would not appear to be on Porto’s side tonight; they have only won two of their last 16 games against English opposition in major European competition.

Team news from Portugal to follow shortly.

#1465. Shambolic off the park, shambolic on it, dire defeat at Falkirk leaves O'Neill on thin ice

Published: 10:28 EDT, 1 November 2026 | Updated: 15:06 EDT, 3 November 2026

It took Celtic supporters the best part of half an hour on Sunday afternoon to belt out their now traditional rendition of ‘Sack the Board, Sack the Board’.

But as dysfunctional as this club may be off the park, there’s no doubt things are every bit as bad on it. This is an organisation that requires a rebuild from top to bottom. No one should be exempt.

Not the board members, not the management team, not the players. The whole thing is a shambles.

The table will show the champions are right on track to defend their crown. Indeed, the stats here will show this was a contest they dominated. But anyone with a set of eyes and any sort of common sense knows the real story.

Ahead of the match, Martin O’Neill insisted he is essentially oblivious to the outside noise around his team. Aye right.

Callum McGregor looks frustrated as Celtic go down in Falkirk

Scott Tanser celebrates his goal with Falkirk team-mate Owen Eames

Legend at the club though he may be, the Northern Irishman is surely on thin ice. Any other Celtic manager with three wins in his last 10 in all competitions certainly would be.

Frankly, he’s kidding himself on when he says he’s been satisfied with Celtic’s start to the season. The fans aren’t buying that nonsense any more. Does the man himself even believe it?

He continually talks about how his team need time to find their feet. More drivel. We’re now in November. Falkirk also signed 17 in the summer and they seem to be doing relatively well.

The football is just atrocious to watch. It has been all season. Such is the standard of the opposition in Scotland, they usually have just about enough quality to get away with it.

But that’s not a long-term solution to an increasingly worrying problem.

Falkirk, by the way, were outstanding here. They have now won four games on the bounce, each in a thoroughly un-Falkirk way.

Their success under John McGlynn has been built on the ability to pass teams off the park. This victory was far more to do with grit, determination and unity than anything else. Three qualities their opponents are lacking.

Falkirk play like a team. Celtic play like a bunch of individuals. And unless something changes pronto, things are going to get even uglier.

Just as they did in the 2-1 win over Hibernian at Easter Road last week, Celtic fell behind early doors.

Finley Barbrook picked up a loose ball midway inside the visitors’ half before finding Ryan Strain in acres of space on the right-hand side.

The full-back’s cross should have been blootered clear by Cameron Carter-Vickers at the back post with minimal fuss. Goodness knows what he actually tried to do, with the ball simply bouncing off the big American and right into the path of the grateful Ethan Ross, who couldn’t miss from five yards out.

Celtic winger Haissem Hassan gets involved in a scuffle with Falkirk players

Shocking stuff from a Celtic perspective. Carter-Vickers’ comments questioning Celtic’s ‘random’ style following defeats to Rangers in September were bang on the money. But he would do well to examine his own performances too. He’s not as good as some fans seem to think.

It took 10 minutes for Celtic to muster up a response. Liam Scales’ long ball found Camilo Duran in behind the Falkirk defence. His strike across goal from a tight angle beat Scott Bain, but not the far post.

Haissem Hassan’s curler from the follow-up was then brilliantly tipped round the post by the keeper.

Jacob Murrell is the country’s in-form striker with five goals in his last seven outings, but sclaffed a shot wide from the penalty spot at the end of a lovely move involving Owen Eames and Scott Tanser down at the corner flag.

Duran should have levelled things up on the half-hour mark after getting on the end of a wicked Hassan ball into the six-yard box, but headed straight at Bain. Anywhere else but right down the middle would have done the trick.

He was made to pay for that miss as Falkirk doubled their advantage with a wonderful team goal on 38 minutes. Eames was given far too much space on the Falkirk left, but take nothing away from the way he threaded an inch-perfect pass into the path of the underlapping Tanser.

He took one touch to set himself as he drove into the box before coolly slotting past Johnstone. It was the kind of football we’ve become accustomed to seeing on a weekly basis from this side under John McGlynn.

Yes, Celtic looked like they couldn’t even be bothered to try and stop them but that’s not Falkirk’s problem. Their execution was flawless.

Man-of-the-Match Bain was once again called into action as the break came into view, and he once again stepped up, tipping Duran’s left-footed strike from 18 yards around the post.

Martin O'Neill looks on in dismay as Celtic suffer in Falkirk

O’Neill could have taken off any one of his so-called big-name stars at half-time and there would have been no grounds for complaint. He settled for just the one, replacing Callum Osmand with James Forrest.

Osmand should never be playing on the wing anyway. In Yang Hyun-Jun’s absence – and with Jota still searching for fitness – he has had a run of games in that position. You suspect he won’t be holding on to it for long. Square pegs in round holes, and all that.

If O’Neill did give his players a boot up the backside at the interval, you wouldn’t have known it, conceding a shocking third through Murrell within minutes of the restart. Fortunately for the visitors, they got away with it, with VAR spotting that the ball was bundled in by the striker’s hand.

Forrest forced a comfortable stop from Bain on the half-turn, with Callum McGregor then blazing over from a promising position.

The captain has been a shadow of himself all season. In truth, he looks a yard or two off the pace.

For so long, we’ve heard that Celtic just can’t do without him. However, playing like this, he isn’t helping this team.

Bain’s stop to deny Forrest on 68 minutes was simple enough. The one which denied substitute Benjamin Nygren seconds later to seal the points was right out of the top drawer.

The Bairns hadn’t beaten Celtic in 19 years coming into this one. Given the state of this Celtic side, is anyone truly surprised that run has come to a halt?
